1|=================
2|Werkzeug Tutorial
3|=================
4|
5|.. currentmodule:: werkzeug
6|
7|Welcome to the Werkzeug tutorial in which we will create a `TinyURL`_ clone
8|that stores URLs in a redis instance.  The libraries we will use for this
9|applications are `Jinja`_ 2 for the templates, `redis`_ for the database
10|layer and, of course, Werkzeug for the WSGI layer.
11|
12|You can use `pip` to install the required libraries::
13|
14|    pip install Jinja2 redis Werkzeug
15|
16|Also make sure to have a redis server running on your local machine.  If
17|you are on OS X, you can use `brew` to install it::
18|
19|    brew install redis
20|
21|If you are on Ubuntu or Debian, you can use apt-get::
22|
23|    sudo apt-get install redis-server
24|
25|Redis was developed for UNIX systems and was never really designed to
26|work on Windows.  For development purposes, the unofficial ports however
27|work well enough.  You can get them from `github
28|<https://github.com/dmajkic/redis/downloads>`_.
29|
30|Introducing Shortly
31|-------------------
32|
33|In this tutorial, we will together create a simple URL shortener service
34|with Werkzeug.  Please keep in mind that Werkzeug is not a framework, it's
35|a library with utilities to create your own framework or application and
36|as such is very flexible.  The approach we use here is just one of many you
37|can use.
38|
39|As data store, we will use `redis`_ here instead of a relational database
40|to keep this simple and because that's the kind of job that `redis`_
41|excels at.
42|
43|The final result will look something like this:
44|
45|.. image:: _static/shortly.png
46|   :alt: a screenshot of shortly
47|
48|.. _TinyURL: https://tinyurl.com/
49|.. _Jinja: http://jinja.pocoo.org/
50|.. _redis: https://redis.io/
51|
52|Step 0: A Basic WSGI Introduction
53|---------------------------------
54|
55|Werkzeug is a utility library for WSGI.  WSGI itself is a protocol or
56|convention that ensures that your web application can speak with the
57|webserver and more importantly that web applications work nicely together.
58|
59|A basic “Hello World” application in WSGI without the help of Werkzeug
60|looks like this::
61|
62|    def application(environ, start_response):
63|        start_response('200 OK', [('Content-Type', 'text/plain')])
64|        return ['Hello World!'.encode('utf-8')]
65|
66|A WSGI application is something you can call and pass an environ dict
67|and a ``start_response`` callable.  The environ contains all incoming
68|information, the ``start_response`` function can be used to indicate the
69|start of the response.  With Werkzeug you don't have to deal directly with
70|either as request and response objects are provided to work with them.
71|
72|The request data takes the environ object and allows you to access the
73|data from that environ in a nice manner.  The response object is a WSGI
74|application in itself and provides a much nicer way to create responses.
75|
76|Here is how you would write that application with response objects::
77|
78|    from werkzeug.wrappers import Response
79|
80|    def application(environ, start_response):
81|        response = Response('Hello World!', mimetype='text/plain')
82|        return response(environ, start_response)
83|
84|And here an expanded version that looks at the query string in the URL
85|(more importantly at the `name` parameter in the URL to substitute “World”
86|against another word)::
87|
88|    from werkzeug.wrappers import Request, Response
89|
90|    def application(environ, start_response):
91|        request = Request(environ)
92|        text = f"Hello {request.args.get('name', 'World')}!"
93|        response = Response(text, mimetype='text/plain')
94|        return response(environ, start_response)
95|
96|And that's all you need to know about WSGI.
97|
98|
99|Step 1: Creating the Folders
100|----------------------------
101|
102|Before we get started, let’s create the folders needed for this application::
103|
104|    /shortly
105|        /static
106|        /templates
107|
108|The shortly folder is not a python package, but just something where we
109|drop our files.  Directly into this folder we will then put our main
110|module in the following steps. The files inside the static folder are
111|available to users of the application via HTTP.  This is the place where
112|CSS and JavaScript files go. Inside the templates folder we will make
113|Jinja2 look for templates.  The templates you create later in the tutorial
114|will go in this directory.
115|
116|Step 2: The Base Structure
117|--------------------------
118|
119|Now let's get right into it and create a module for our application.  Let's
120|create a file called `shortly.py` in the `shortly` folder.  At first we
121|will need a bunch of imports.  I will pull in all the imports here, even
122|if they are not used right away, to keep it from being confusing::
123|
124|    import os
125|    import redis
126|    from urllib.parse import urlparse
127|    from werkzeug.wrappers import Request, Response
128|    from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule
129|    from werkzeug.exceptions import HTTPException, NotFound
130|    from werkzeug.middleware.shared_data import SharedDataMiddleware
131|    from werkzeug.utils import redirect
132|    from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
133|
134|Then we can create the basic structure for our application and a function
135|to create a new instance of it, optionally with a piece of WSGI middleware
136|that exports all the files on the `static` folder on the web::
137|
138|    class Shortly(object):
139|
140|        def __init__(self, config):
141|            self.redis = redis.Redis(
142|                config['redis_host'], config['redis_port'], decode_responses=True
143|            )
144|
145|        def dispatch_request(self, request):
146|            return Response('Hello World!')
147|
148|        def wsgi_app(self, environ, start_response):
149|            request = Request(environ)
150|            response = self.dispatch_request(request)
151|            return response(environ, start_response)
152|
153|        def __call__(self, environ, start_response):
154|            return self.wsgi_app(environ, start_response)
155|
156|
157|    def create_app(redis_host='localhost', redis_port=6379, with_static=True):
158|        app = Shortly({
159|            'redis_host':       redis_host,
160|            'redis_port':       redis_port
161|        })
162|        if with_static:
163|            app.wsgi_app = SharedDataMiddleware(app.wsgi_app, {
164|                '/static':  os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), 'static')
165|            })
166|        return app
167|
168|Lastly we can add a piece of code that will start a local development
169|server with automatic code reloading and a debugger::
170|
171|    if __name__ == '__main__':
172|        from werkzeug.serving import run_simple
173|        app = create_app()
174|        run_simple('127.0.0.1', 5000, app, use_debugger=True, use_reloader=True)
175|
176|The basic idea here is that our ``Shortly`` class is an actual WSGI
177|application.  The ``__call__`` method directly dispatches to ``wsgi_app``.
178|This is done so that we can wrap ``wsgi_app`` to apply middlewares like we
179|do in the ``create_app`` function.  The actual ``wsgi_app`` method then
180|creates a :class:`Request` object and calls the ``dispatch_request``
181|method which then has to return a :class:`Response` object which is then
182|evaluated as WSGI application again.  As you can see: turtles all the way
183|down.  Both the ``Shortly`` class we create, as well as any request object
184|in Werkzeug implements the WSGI interface.  As a result of that you could
185|even return another WSGI application from the ``dispatch_request`` method.
186|
187|The ``create_app`` factory function can be used to create a new instance
188|of our application.  Not only will it pass some parameters as
189|configuration to the application but also optionally add a WSGI middleware
190|that exports static files.  This way we have access to the files from the
191|static folder even when we are not configuring our server to provide them
192|which is very helpful for development.
193|
194|Intermezzo: Running the Application
195|-----------------------------------
196|
197|Now you should be able to execute the file with `python` and see a server
198|on your local machine::
199|
200|    $ python shortly.py
201|     * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/
202|     * Restarting with reloader: stat() polling
203|
204|It also tells you that the reloader is active.  It will use various
205|techniques to figure out if any file changed on the disk and then
206|automatically restart.
207|
208|Just go to the URL and you should see “Hello World!”.
209|
210|Step 3: The Environment
211|-----------------------
212|
213|Now that we have the basic application class, we can make the constructor
214|do something useful and provide a few helpers on there that can come in
215|handy.  We will need to be able to render templates and connect to redis,
216|so let's extend the class a bit::
217|
218|    def __init__(self, config):
219|        self.redis = redis.Redis(config['redis_host'], config['redis_port'])
220|        template_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), 'templates')
221|        self.jinja_env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader(template_path),
222|                                     autoescape=True)
223|
224|    def render_template(self, template_name, **context):
225|        t = self.jinja_env.get_template(template_name)
226|        return Response(t.render(context), mimetype='text/html')
227|
228|Step 4: The Routing
229|-------------------
230|
231|Next up is routing.  Routing is the process of matching and parsing the URL to
232|something we can use.  Werkzeug provides a flexible integrated routing
233|system which we can use for that.  The way it works is that you create a
234|:class:`~werkzeug.routing.Map` instance and add a bunch of
235|:class:`~werkzeug.routing.Rule` objects.  Each rule has a pattern it will
236|try to match the URL against and an “endpoint”.  The endpoint is typically
237|a string and can be used to uniquely identify the URL.  We could also use
238|this to automatically reverse the URL, but that's not what we will do in this
239|tutorial.
240|
241|Just put this into the constructor::
242|
243|    self.url_map = Map([
244|        Rule('/', endpoint='new_url'),
245|        Rule('/<short_id>', endpoint='follow_short_link'),
246|        Rule('/<short_id>+', endpoint='short_link_details')
247|    ])
248|
249|Here we create a URL map with three rules.  ``/`` for the root of the URL
250|space where we will just dispatch to a function that implements the logic
251|to create a new URL.  And then one that follows the short link to the
252|target URL and another one with the same rule but a plus (``+``) at the
253|end to show the link details.
254|
255|So how do we find our way from the endpoint to a function?  That's up to you.
256|The way we will do it in this tutorial is by calling the method ``on_``
257|+ endpoint on the class itself.  Here is how this works::
258|
259|    def dispatch_request(self, request):
260|        adapter = self.url_map.bind_to_environ(request.environ)
261|        try:
262|            endpoint, values = adapter.match()
263|            return getattr(self, f'on_{endpoint}')(request, **values)
264|        except HTTPException as e:
265|            return e
266|
267|We bind the URL map to the current environment and get back a
268|:class:`~werkzeug.routing.MapAdapter`.  The adapter can be used to match
269|the request but also to reverse URLs.  The match method will return the
270|endpoint and a dictionary of values in the URL.  For instance the rule for
271|``follow_short_link`` has a variable part called ``short_id``.  When we go
272|to ``http://localhost:5000/foo`` we will get the following values back::
273|
274|    endpoint = 'follow_short_link'
275|    values = {'short_id': 'foo'}
276|
277|If it does not match anything, it will raise a
278|:exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.NotFound` exception, which is an
279|:exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.HTTPException`.  All HTTP exceptions are also
280|WSGI applications by themselves which render a default error page.  So we
281|just catch all of them down and return the error itself.
282|
283|If all works well, we call the function ``on_`` + endpoint and pass it the
284|request as argument as well as all the URL arguments as keyword arguments
285|and return the response object that method returns.
286|
287|Step 5: The First View
288|----------------------
289|
290|Let's start with the first view: the one for new URLs::
291|
292|    def on_new_url(self, request):
293|        error = None
294|        url = ''
295|        if request.method == 'POST':
296|            url = request.form['url']
297|            if not is_valid_url(url):
298|                error = 'Please enter a valid URL'
299|            else:
300|                short_id = self.insert_url(url)
301|                return redirect(f"/{short_id}+")
302|        return self.render_template('new_url.html', error=error, url=url)
303|
304|This logic should be easy to understand.  Basically we are checking that
305|the request method is POST, in which case we validate the URL and add a
306|new entry to the database, then redirect to the detail page.  This means
307|we need to write a function and a helper method.  For URL validation this
308|is good enough::
309|
310|    def is_valid_url(url):
311|        parts = urlparse(url)
312|        return parts.scheme in ('http', 'https')
313|
314|For inserting the URL, all we need is this little method on our class::
315|
316|    def insert_url(self, url):
317|        short_id = self.redis.get(f'reverse-url:{url}')
318|        if short_id is not None:
319|            return short_id
320|        url_num = self.redis.incr('last-url-id')
321|        short_id = base36_encode(url_num)
322|        self.redis.set(f'url-target:{short_id}', url)
323|        self.redis.set(f'reverse-url:{url}', short_id)
324|        return short_id
325|
326|``reverse-url:`` + the URL will store the short id.  If the URL was
327|already submitted this won't be None and we can just return that value
328|which will be the short ID.  Otherwise we increment the ``last-url-id``
329|key and convert it to base36.  Then we store the link and the reverse
330|entry in redis.  And here the function to convert to base 36::
331|
332|    def base36_encode(number):
333|        assert number >= 0, 'positive integer required'
334|        if number == 0:
335|            return '0'
336|        base36 = []
337|        while number != 0:
338|            number, i = divmod(number, 36)
339|            base36.append('0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'[i])
340|        return ''.join(reversed(base36))
341|
342|So what is missing for this view to work is the template.  We will create
343|this later, let's first also write the other views and then do the
344|templates in one go.
345|
346|Step 6: Redirect View
347|---------------------
348|
349|The redirect view is easy.  All it has to do is to look for the link in
350|redis and redirect to it.  Additionally we will also increment a counter
351|so that we know how often a link was clicked::
352|
353|    def on_follow_short_link(self, request, short_id):
354|        link_target = self.redis.get(f'url-target:{short_id}')
355|        if link_target is None:
356|            raise NotFound()
357|        self.redis.incr(f'click-count:{short_id}')
358|        return redirect(link_target)
359|
360|In this case we will raise a :exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.NotFound` exception
361|by hand if the URL does not exist, which will bubble up to the
362|``dispatch_request`` function and be converted into a default 404
363|response.
364|
365|Step 7: Detail View
366|-------------------
367|
368|The link detail view is very similar, we just render a template
369|again.  In addition to looking up the target, we also ask redis for the
370|number of times the link was clicked and let it default to zero if such
371|a key does not yet exist::
372|
373|    def on_short_link_details(self, request, short_id):
374|        link_target = self.redis.get(f'url-target:{short_id}')
375|        if link_target is None:
376|            raise NotFound()
377|        click_count = int(self.redis.get(f'click-count:{short_id}') or 0)
378|        return self.render_template('short_link_details.html',
379|            link_target=link_target,
380|            short_id=short_id,
381|            click_count=click_count
382|        )
383|
384|Please be aware that redis always works with strings, so you have to convert
385|the click count to :class:`int` by hand.
386|
387|Step 8: Templates
388|-----------------
389|
390|And here are all the templates.  Just drop them into the `templates`
391|folder.  Jinja2 supports template inheritance, so the first thing we will
392|do is create a layout template with blocks that act as placeholders.  We
393|also set up Jinja2 so that it automatically escapes strings with HTML
394|rules, so we don't have to spend time on that ourselves.  This prevents
395|XSS attacks and rendering errors.
396|
397|*layout.html*:
398|
399|.. sourcecode:: html+jinja
400|
401|    <!doctype html>
402|    <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %} | shortly</title>
403|    <link rel=stylesheet href=/static/style.css type=text/css>
404|    <div class=box>
405|      <h1><a href=/>shortly</a></h1>
406|      <p class=tagline>Shortly is a URL shortener written with Werkzeug
407|      {% block body %}{% endblock %}
408|    </div>
409|
410|*new_url.html*:
411|
412|.. sourcecode:: html+jinja
413|
414|    {% extends "layout.html" %}
415|    {% block title %}Create New Short URL{% endblock %}
416|    {% block body %}
417|      <h2>Submit URL</h2>
418|      <form action="" method=post>
419|        {% if error %}
420|          <p class=error><strong>Error:</strong> {{ error }}
421|        {% endif %}

423|          <input type=text name=url value="{{ url }}" class=urlinput>
424|          <input type=submit value="Shorten">
425|      </form>
426|    {% endblock %}
427|
428|*short_link_details.html*:
429|
430|.. sourcecode:: html+jinja
431|
432|    {% extends "layout.html" %}
433|    {% block title %}Details about /{{ short_id }}{% endblock %}
434|    {% block body %}
435|      <h2><a href="/{{ short_id }}">/{{ short_id }}</a></h2>
436|      <dl>
437|        <dt>Full link
438|        <dd class=link><div>{{ link_target }}</div>

440|        <dd>{{ click_count }}

442|    {% endblock %}

1|===========
2|URL Routing
3|===========
4|
5|.. module:: werkzeug.routing
6|
7|When it comes to combining multiple controller or view functions (however
8|you want to call them), you need a dispatcher.  A simple way would be
9|applying regular expression tests on ``PATH_INFO`` and call registered
10|callback functions that return the value.
11|
12|Werkzeug provides a much more powerful system, similar to `Routes`_.  All the
13|objects mentioned on this page must be imported from :mod:`werkzeug.routing`, not
14|from :mod:`werkzeug`!
15|
16|.. _Routes: https://routes.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
17|
18|
19|Quickstart
20|==========
21|
22|Here is a simple example which could be the URL definition for a blog::
23|
24|    from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule, NotFound, RequestRedirect
25|
26|    url_map = Map([
27|        Rule('/', endpoint='blog/index'),
28|        Rule('/<int:year>/', endpoint='blog/archive'),
29|        Rule('/<int:year>/<int:month>/', endpoint='blog/archive'),
30|        Rule('/<int:year>/<int:month>/<int:day>/', endpoint='blog/archive'),
31|        Rule('/<int:year>/<int:month>/<int:day>/<slug>',
32|             endpoint='blog/show_post'),
33|        Rule('/about', endpoint='blog/about_me'),
34|        Rule('/feeds/', endpoint='blog/feeds'),
35|        Rule('/feeds/<feed_name>.rss', endpoint='blog/show_feed')
36|    ])
37|
38|    def application(environ, start_response):
39|        urls = url_map.bind_to_environ(environ)
40|        try:
41|            endpoint, args = urls.match()
42|        except HTTPException as e:
43|            return e(environ, start_response)
44|        start_response('200 OK', [('Content-Type', 'text/plain')])
45|        return [f'Rule points to {endpoint!r} with arguments {args!r}'.encode()]
46|
47|So what does that do?  First of all we create a new :class:`Map` which stores
48|a bunch of URL rules.  Then we pass it a list of :class:`Rule` objects.
49|
50|Each :class:`Rule` object is instantiated with a string that represents a rule
51|and an endpoint which will be the alias for what view the rule represents.
52|Multiple rules can have the same endpoint, but should have different arguments
53|to allow URL construction.
54|
55|The format for the URL rules is straightforward, but explained in detail below.
56|
57|Inside the WSGI application we bind the url_map to the current request which will
58|return a new :class:`MapAdapter`.  This url_map adapter can then be used to match
59|or build domains for the current request.
60|
61|The :meth:`MapAdapter.match` method can then either return a tuple in the form
62|``(endpoint, args)`` or raise one of the three exceptions
63|:exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.NotFound`, :exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.MethodNotAllowed`,
64|or :exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.RequestRedirect`.  For more details about those
65|exceptions have a look at the documentation of the :meth:`MapAdapter.match` method.
66|
67|
68|Rule Format
69|===========
70|
71|Rule strings are URL paths with placeholders for variable parts in the
72|format ``<converter(arguments):name>``. ``converter`` and ``arguments``
73|(with parentheses) are optional. If no converter is given, the
74|``default`` converter is used (``string`` by default). The available
75|converters are discussed below.
76|
77|Rule path parts are separated by ``/`` and matched individually, unless a
78|converter opts in to matching ``/`` as well.
79|
80|Rules that end with a slash are "branches", others are "leaves". If
81|``strict_slashes`` is enabled (the default), visiting a branch URL
82|without a trailing slash will redirect to the URL with a slash appended.
83|
84|Many HTTP servers merge consecutive slashes into one when receiving
85|requests. If ``merge_slashes`` is enabled (the default), rules will
86|merge slashes in non-variable parts when matching and building. Visiting
87|a URL with consecutive slashes will redirect to the URL with slashes
88|merged. If you want to disable ``merge_slashes`` for a :class:`Rule` or
89|:class:`Map`, you'll also need to configure your web server
90|appropriately.
91|
92|Besides the path, matching can also use the subdomain of a known base domain if
93|``subdomain_matching`` is enabled (the default), or the full host (if
94|``host_matching`` is enabled). The subdomain or host parts can also contain
95|variables. Unlike the path, where multiple parts are separated by ``/``, the
96|domain is always matched as a single part.
97|
98|If a duplicate rule is added to a map, a :exc:`.DuplicateRuleError` will be
99|raised. Rules are compared based on their path, subdomain or host, websocket
100|mode, and methods. Variable parts are not equal if they use different
101|converters, although this heuristic may not be perfect depending on what the
102|different converters can actually match. Rules with equal or overlapping (but
103|not exactly equal) methods are considered duplicates. The ``HEAD`` and
104|``OPTIONS`` methods are not considered for the overlapping check, only for exact
105|equality, as they are typically added automatically.
106|
107|
108|Rule Priority
109|=============
110|
111|In general, the map matches more specific rules first. Rules are made up of
112|static and variable parts, separated by slash ``/``. For a given segment, rules
113|with a static part in that position take priority, and longer static values take
114|priority over shorter. Variable parts are weighted based on the type of data
115|they match.
116|
117|If you're using subdomain or host matching, the domain part can use converters
118|as well. The domain part is matched before the path parts. Like the path parts,
119|a static domain part take priority over a variable part.
120|
121|Rules may end up with the same priority, by having static parts with the same
122|length, and dynamic parts with the same weight, in the same positions. In this
123|case, sorting is stable, so rules added earlier take priority.
124|
125|The exact way that rules are sorted internally is pretty complicated, but the
126|result should be that you can rely on more specific rules matching before more
127|general ones.
128|
129|
130|Built-in Converters
131|===================
132|
133|Converters for common types of URL variables are built-in. The available
134|converters can be overridden or extended through :attr:`Map.converters`.
135|
136|.. autoclass:: UnicodeConverter
137|
138|.. autoclass:: PathConverter
139|
140|.. autoclass:: AnyConverter
141|
142|.. autoclass:: IntegerConverter
143|
144|.. autoclass:: FloatConverter

150|========================
151|

195|
196|Custom Converters
197|=================
198|
199|You can add custom converters that add behaviors not provided by the
200|built-in converters. To make a custom converter, subclass
201|:class:`BaseConverter` then pass the new class to the :class:`Map`
202|``converters`` parameter, or add it to
203|:attr:`url_map.converters <Map.converters>`.
204|
205|The converter should have a ``regex`` attribute with a regular
206|expression to match with. If the converter can take arguments in a URL
207|rule, it should accept them in its ``__init__`` method. The entire
208|regex expression will be matched as a group and used as the value for
209|conversion.
210|
211|If a custom converter can match a forward slash, ``/``, it should have
212|the attribute ``part_isolating`` set to ``False``. This will ensure
213|that rules using the custom converter are correctly matched.
214|
215|It can implement a ``to_python`` method to convert the matched string to
216|some other object. This can also do extra validation that wasn't
217|possible with the ``regex`` attribute, and should raise a
218|:exc:`werkzeug.routing.ValidationError` in that case. Raising any other
219|errors will cause a 500 error.
220|
221|It can implement a ``to_url`` method to convert a Python object to a
222|string when building a URL. Any error raised here will be converted to a
223|:exc:`werkzeug.routing.BuildError` and eventually cause a 500 error.
224|
225|This example implements a ``BooleanConverter`` that will match the
226|strings ``"yes"``, ``"no"``, and ``"maybe"``, returning a random value
227|for ``"maybe"``. ::
228|
229|    from random import randrange
230|    from werkzeug.routing import BaseConverter, ValidationError
231|
232|    class BooleanConverter(BaseConverter):
233|        regex = r"(?:yes|no|maybe)"
234|
235|        def __init__(self, url_map, maybe=False):
236|            super().__init__(url_map)
237|            self.maybe = maybe
238|
239|        def to_python(self, value):
240|            if value == "maybe":
241|                if self.maybe:
242|                    return not randrange(2)
243|                raise ValidationError
244|            return value == 'yes'
245|
246|        def to_url(self, value):
247|            return "yes" if value else "no"
248|
249|    from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule
250|
251|    url_map = Map([
252|        Rule("/vote/<bool:werkzeug_rocks>", endpoint="vote"),
253|        Rule("/guess/<bool(maybe=True):foo>", endpoint="guess")
254|    ], converters={'bool': BooleanConverter})
255|
256|If you want to change the default converter, assign a different
257|converter to the ``"default"`` key.
258|
259|
260|Subdomain or Host Matching
261|==========================
262|
263|It's possible to route based on the domain part of the URL, in addition
264|to the path. There are two ways to match, by subdomains under a single domain,
265|or by full domains.
266|
267|Subdomain Matching
268|------------------
269|
270|Subdomain matching is the more common approach, and is enabled by default.
271|In order to route by subdomain, pass the ``subdomain`` argument to
272|:class:`Rule`. It can use converters just like the path part of the rule can.
273|
274|.. code-block:: python
275|
276|    from werkzeug import Request, Response
277|    from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule
278|
279|    url_map = Map([
280|        Rule("/", endpoint="base"),
281|        Rule("/", endpoint="support", subdomain="support"),
282|        Rule("/<word>", endpoint="word", subdomain="<language>"),
283|    ])
284|
285|    @Request.application
286|    def app(request: Request) -> Response:
287|        urls = url_map.bind_to_environ(request, server_name="app.example")
288|        endpoint, args = urls.match()
289|        # for the word endpoint, args will contain "language" and "word"
290|        ...
291|
292|You can also use the :class:`Subdomain` rule factory to apply a subdomain rule
293|automatically to a list of rules.
294|
295|If a rule doesn't specify a ``subdomain`` part, it will use the
296|:attr:`Map.default_subdomain`. This defaults to empty, meaning it will match on
297|the base domain only. In order for the routing to know the subdomain, you must
298|pass the base ``server_name`` when calling :meth:`Map.bind_to_environ`. If the
299|map cannot determine the subdomain, such as when accessing by IP or an alternate
300|domain name, it will also default to :attr:`Map.default_subdomain`.
301|
302|It's also possible to disable any domain-based routing, by passing
303|``subdomain_matching=False`` when creating the :class:`Map` (``host_matching``
304|defaults to false).
305|
306|Host Matching
307|-------------
308|
309|If your application is intended to be accessed from separate domains, rather
310|than subdomains, you can use host matching instead. Pass ``host_matching=True``
311|when creating the :class:`Map` to enable it, and pass the ``host`` argument to
312|:class:`Rule`. It can use converters just like the path part of the rule can.
313|
314|.. code-block:: python
315|
316|    from werkzeug import Request, Response
317|    from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule
318|
319|    url_map = Map([
320|        Rule("/", endpoint="company", host="company.example"),
321|        Rule("/", endpoint="user", host="<user>.app.example"),
322|    ])
323|
324|    @Request.application
325|    def app(request: Request) -> Response:
326|        urls = url_map.bind_to_environ(request)
327|        endpoint, args = urls.match()
328|        # for the user endpoint, args will contain "user"
329|        ...
330|
331|Enabling ``host_matching`` disables ``subdomain_matching``, as matching
332|subdomains is a subset of matching hosts. That is, if you also want to match
333|subdomains, you still can by specifying the full domain rather than only the
334|prefix.
335|
336|The ``Host`` header used for this matching also includes the port if it's
337|non-standard (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443). This means that you can route based on port
338|as well; however it also means that when running the development server the port
339|will be 5000 (by default) and the rules would need to be updated. You could
340|write a small helper to append the correct port based on configuration when
341|creating rules, or you could add an HTTP server as described in
342|:doc:`deployment/index` to proxy the port.
343|
344|
345|WebSockets
346|==========
347|
348|.. versionadded:: 1.0
349|
350|If a :class:`Rule` is created with ``websocket=True``, it will only
351|match if the :class:`Map` is bound to a request with a ``url_scheme`` of
352|``ws`` or ``wss``.
353|
354|.. note::
355|
356|   Werkzeug has no further WebSocket support beyond routing. This
357|   functionality is mostly of use to ASGI projects.
358|
359|.. code-block:: python
360|
361|    url_map = Map([
362|        Rule("/ws", endpoint="comm", websocket=True),
363|    ])
364|    adapter = map.bind("example.org", "/ws", url_scheme="ws")
365|    assert adapter.match() == ("comm", {})
366|
367|If the only match is a WebSocket rule and the bind is HTTP (or the
368|only match is HTTP and the bind is WebSocket) a
369|:exc:`WebsocketMismatch` (derives from
370|:exc:`~werkzeug.exceptions.BadRequest`) exception is raised.
371|
372|As WebSocket URLs have a different scheme, rules are always built with a
373|scheme and host, ``force_external=True`` is implied.
374|
375|.. code-block:: python
376|
377|    url = adapter.build("comm")
378|    assert url == "ws://example.org/ws"

2|Basic HTTP Proxy

11|from __future__ import annotations

13|import typing as t
14|import wsgiref.types as wt
15|from http import client
16|from urllib.parse import quote
17|from urllib.parse import urlsplit
18|
19|from .. import Request
20|from .. import Response
21|from ..datastructures import Headers
22|from ..datastructures import HeaderSet
23|from ..exceptions import BadGateway
24|from ..http import is_hop_by_hop_header
25|
26|
27|class ProxyMiddleware:
28|    """Proxy requests under a path to an external server, routing other
29|    requests to the app.
30|
31|    This middleware can only proxy HTTP requests, as HTTP is the only
32|    protocol handled by the WSGI server. Other protocols, such as
33|    WebSocket requests, cannot be proxied at this layer. This should
34|    only be used for development, in production a real proxy server
35|    should be used.
36|
37|    The middleware takes a dict mapping a path prefix to a dict
38|    describing the host to be proxied to::
39|
40|        app = ProxyMiddleware(app, {
41|            "/static/": {
42|                "target": "http://127.0.0.1:5001/",
43|            }
44|        })
45|
46|    Each host has the following options:
47|
48|    ``target``:
49|        The target URL to dispatch to. This is required.
50|    ``remove_prefix``:
51|        Whether to remove the prefix from the URL before dispatching it
52|        to the target. The default is ``False``.
53|    ``host``:
54|        ``"<auto>"`` (default):
55|            The host header is automatically rewritten to the URL of the
56|            target.
57|        ``None``:
58|            The host header is unmodified from the client request.
59|        Any other value:
60|            The host header is overwritten with the value.
61|    ``headers``:
62|        A dictionary of headers to be sent with the request to the
63|        target. The default is ``{}``.
64|    ``ssl_context``:
65|        A :class:`ssl.SSLContext` defining how to verify requests if the
66|        target is HTTPS. The default is ``None``.
67|
68|    In the example above, everything under ``"/static/"`` is proxied to
69|    the server on port 5001. The host header is rewritten to the target,
70|    and the ``"/static/"`` prefix is removed from the URLs.
71|
72|    :param app: The WSGI application to wrap.
73|    :param targets: Proxy target configurations. See description above.
74|    :param chunk_size: Size of chunks to read from input stream and
75|        write to target.
76|    :param timeout: Seconds before an operation to a target fails.
77|
78|    .. versionadded:: 0.14
79|    """
80|
81|    def __init__(
82|        self,
83|        app: wt.WSGIApplication,
84|        targets: t.Mapping[str, dict[str, t.Any]],
85|        chunk_size: int = 2 << 13,
86|        timeout: int = 10,
87|    ) -> None:
88|        def _set_defaults(opts: dict[str, t.Any]) -> dict[str, t.Any]:
89|            opts.setdefault("remove_prefix", False)
90|            opts.setdefault("host", "<auto>")
91|            opts.setdefault("headers", {})
92|            opts.setdefault("ssl_context", None)
93|            return opts
94|
95|        self.app = app
96|        self.targets = {
97|            f"/{k.strip('/')}/": _set_defaults(v) for k, v in targets.items()
98|        }
99|        self.chunk_size = chunk_size
100|        self.timeout = timeout
101|
102|    def proxy_to(
103|        self, opts: dict[str, t.Any], path: str, prefix: str
104|    ) -> wt.WSGIApplication:
105|        target = urlsplit(opts["target"])
106|        # socket can handle unicode host, but header must be ascii
107|        host = target.hostname.encode("idna").decode("ascii")
108|
109|        @Request.application
110|        def application(request: Request) -> wt.WSGIApplication:
111|            connection_header = HeaderSet.from_header(request.headers.get("Connection"))
112|            headers = Headers(
113|                (k, v)
114|                for k, v in request.headers.items()
115|                if not is_hop_by_hop_header(k, connection_header)
116|            )
117|            headers["Connection"] = "close"
118|
119|            if opts["host"] == "<auto>":
120|                headers["Host"] = host
121|            elif opts["host"] is None:
122|                headers["Host"] = request.host
123|            else:
124|                headers["Host"] = opts["host"]
125|
126|            headers.extend(opts["headers"])
127|            remote_path = path
128|
129|            if opts["remove_prefix"]:
130|                remote_path = remote_path[len(prefix) :].lstrip("/")
131|                remote_path = f"{target.path.rstrip('/')}/{remote_path}"
132|
133|            try:
134|                if target.scheme == "http":
135|                    con = client.HTTPConnection(
136|                        host, target.port or 80, timeout=self.timeout
137|                    )
138|                elif target.scheme == "https":
139|                    con = client.HTTPSConnection(
140|                        host,
141|                        target.port or 443,
142|                        timeout=self.timeout,
143|                        context=opts["ssl_context"],
144|                    )
145|                else:
146|                    raise RuntimeError(
147|                        "Target scheme must be 'http' or 'https', got"
148|                        f" {target.scheme!r}."
149|                    )
150|
151|                con.connect()
152|                # safe = https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-path-segment-string
153|                # as well as percent for things that are already quoted
154|                remote_url = quote(remote_path, safe="!$&'()*+,/:;=@%")
155|
156|                if request.query_string:
157|                    remote_url = f"{remote_url}?{request.query_string.decode()}"
158|
159|                con.putrequest(request.method, remote_url, skip_host=True)
160|
161|                for k, v in headers.items():
162|                    con.putheader(k, v)
163|
164|                con.endheaders()
165|
166|                while data := request.stream.read(self.chunk_size):
167|                    con.send(data)
168|
169|                resp = con.getresponse()
170|            except OSError as e:
171|                raise BadGateway from e
172|
173|            headers = Headers(resp.getheaders())
174|            connection_header = HeaderSet.from_header(headers.get("Connection"))
175|            headers = Headers(
176|                (k, v)
177|                for k, v in headers
178|                if not is_hop_by_hop_header(k, connection_header)
179|            )
180|            return Response(resp, status=resp.status, headers=headers)
181|
182|        return application
183|
184|    @Request.application
185|    def __call__(self, request: Request) -> wt.WSGIApplication:
186|        for prefix, opts in self.targets.items():
187|            if request.path.startswith(prefix):
188|                return self.proxy_to(opts, request.path, prefix)
189|
190|        return self.app

--- FILE: docs/quickstart.rst ---
1|Quickstart
2|==========
3|
4|.. currentmodule:: werkzeug
5|
6|This part of the documentation shows how to use the most important parts of
7|Werkzeug.  It's intended as a starting point for developers with basic
8|understanding of :pep:`3333` (WSGI) and :rfc:`2616` (HTTP).
9|
10|
11|WSGI Environment
12|----------------
13|
14|The WSGI environment contains all the information the user request transmits
15|to the application.  It is passed to the WSGI application but you can also
16|create a WSGI environ dict using the :func:`create_environ` helper:
17|
18|>>> from werkzeug.test import create_environ
19|>>> environ = create_environ('/foo', 'http://localhost:8080/')
20|
21|Now we have an environment to play around:
22|
23|>>> environ['PATH_INFO']
24|'/foo'
25|>>> environ['SCRIPT_NAME']
26|''
27|>>> environ['SERVER_NAME']
28|'localhost'
29|
30|Usually nobody wants to work with the environ directly because it uses a
31|confusing string encoding scheme, and it does not provide any way to
32|access the form data besides parsing that data by hand.
33|
34|
35|Enter Request
36|-------------
37|
38|For access to the request data the :class:`Request` object is much more fun.
39|It wraps the `environ` and provides a read-only access to the data from
40|there:
41|
42|>>> from werkzeug.wrappers import Request
43|>>> request = Request(environ)
44|
45|Now you can access the important variables and Werkzeug will parse them
46|for you and decode them where it makes sense.
47|
48|>>> request.path
49|'/foo'
50|>>> request.script_root
51|''
52|>>> request.host
53|'localhost:8080'
54|>>> request.url
55|'http://localhost:8080/foo'
56|
57|We can also find out which HTTP method was used for the request:
58|
59|>>> request.method
60|'GET'
61|
62|This way we can also access URL arguments (the query string) and data that
63|was transmitted in a POST/PUT request.
64|
65|For testing purposes we can create a request object from supplied data
66|using the :meth:`~Request.from_values` method:
67|
68|>>> from io import StringIO
69|>>> data = "name=this+is+encoded+form+data&another_key=another+one"
70|>>> request = Request.from_values(query_string='foo=bar&blah=blafasel',
71|...    content_length=len(data), input_stream=StringIO(data),
72|...    content_type='application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
73|...    method='POST')
74|...
75|>>> request.method
76|'POST'
77|
78|Now we can access the URL parameters easily:
79|
80|>>> request.args.keys()
81|['blah', 'foo']
82|>>> request.args['blah']
83|'blafasel'
84|
85|Same for the supplied form data:
86|
87|>>> request.form['name']
88|'this is encoded form data'
89|
90|Handling for uploaded files is not much harder as you can see from this
91|example::
92|
93|    def store_file(request):
94|        file = request.files.get('my_file')
95|        if file:
96|            file.save('/where/to/store/the/file.txt')
97|        else:
98|            handle_the_error()
99|
100|The files are represented as :class:`FileStorage` objects which provide
101|some common operations to work with them.
102|
103|Request headers can be accessed by using the :class:`~Request.headers`
104|attribute:
105|
106|>>> request.headers['Content-Length']
107|'54'
108|>>> request.headers['Content-Type']
109|'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
110|
111|The keys for the headers are of course case insensitive.
112|
113|
114|Header Parsing
115|--------------
116|
117|There is more.  Werkzeug provides convenient access to often used HTTP headers
118|and other request data.
119|
120|Let's create a request object with all the data a typical web browser transmits
121|so that we can play with it:
122|
123|>>> environ = create_environ()
124|>>> environ.update(
125|...     HTTP_ACCEPT='text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8',
126|...     HTTP_ACCEPT_LANGUAGE='de-at,en-us;q=0.8,en;q=0.5',
127|...     HTTP_ACCEPT_ENCODING='gzip,deflate',
128|...     HTTP_ACCEPT_CHARSET='ISO-8859-1,utf-8;q=0.7,*;q=0.7',
129|...     HTTP_IF_MODIFIED_SINCE='Fri, 20 Feb 2009 10:10:25 GMT',
130|...     HTTP_IF_NONE_MATCH='"e51c9-1e5d-46356dc86c640"',
131|...     HTTP_CACHE_CONTROL='max-age=0'
132|... )
133|...
134|>>> request = Request(environ)
135|
136|With the accept header the browser informs the web application what
137|mimetypes it can handle and how well. All accept headers are sorted by
138|the quality, the best item being the first:
139|
140|>>> request.accept_mimetypes.best
141|'text/html'
142|>>> 'application/xhtml+xml' in request.accept_mimetypes
143|True
144|>>> print(request.accept_mimetypes["application/json"])
145|0.8
146|
147|The same works for languages:
148|
149|>>> request.accept_languages.best
150|'de-at'
151|>>> request.accept_languages.values()
152|['de-at', 'en-us', 'en']
153|
154|And of course encodings and charsets:
155|
156|>>> 'gzip' in request.accept_encodings
157|True
158|>>> request.accept_charsets.best
159|'ISO-8859-1'
160|>>> 'utf-8' in request.accept_charsets
161|True
162|
163|Normalization is available, so you can safely use alternative forms to perform
164|containment checking:
165|
166|>>> 'UTF8' in request.accept_charsets
167|True
168|>>> 'de_AT' in request.accept_languages
169|True
170|
171|E-tags and other conditional headers are available in parsed form as well:
172|
173|>>> request.if_modified_since
174|datetime.datetime(2009, 2, 20, 10, 10, 25, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
175|>>> request.if_none_match
176|<ETags '"e51c9-1e5d-46356dc86c640"'>
177|>>> request.cache_control
178|<RequestCacheControl 'max-age=0'>
179|>>> request.cache_control.max_age
180|0
181|>>> 'e51c9-1e5d-46356dc86c640' in request.if_none_match
182|True
183|
184|
185|Responses
186|---------
187|
188|Response objects are the opposite of request objects.  They are used to send
189|data back to the client.  In reality, response objects are nothing more than
190|glorified WSGI applications.
191|
192|So what you are doing is not *returning* the response objects from your WSGI
193|application but *calling* it as WSGI application inside your WSGI application
194|and returning the return value of that call.
195|
196|So imagine your standard WSGI "Hello World" application::
197|
198|    def application(environ, start_response):
199|        start_response('200 OK', [('Content-Type', 'text/plain')])
200|        return ['Hello World!']
201|
202|With response objects it would look like this::
203|
204|    from werkzeug.wrappers import Response
205|
206|    def application(environ, start_response):
207|        response = Response('Hello World!')
208|        return response(environ, start_response)
209|
210|Also, unlike request objects, response objects are designed to be modified.
211|So here is what you can do with them:
212|
213|>>> from werkzeug.wrappers import Response
214|>>> response = Response("Hello World!")
215|>>> response.headers['content-type']
216|'text/plain; charset=utf-8'
217|>>> response.data
218|'Hello World!'
219|>>> response.headers['content-length'] = len(response.data)
220|
221|You can modify the status of the response in the same way.  Either just the
222|code or provide a message as well:
223|
224|>>> response.status
225|'200 OK'
226|>>> response.status = '404 Not Found'
227|>>> response.status_code
228|404
229|>>> response.status_code = 400
230|>>> response.status
231|'400 BAD REQUEST'
232|
233|As you can see attributes work in both directions.  So you can set both
234|:attr:`~Response.status` and :attr:`~Response.status_code` and the
235|change will be reflected to the other.
236|
237|Also common headers are exposed as attributes or with methods to set /
238|retrieve them:
239|
240|>>> response.content_length
241|12
242|>>> from datetime import datetime, timezone
243|>>> response.date = datetime(2009, 2, 20, 17, 42, 51, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
244|>>> response.headers['Date']
245|'Fri, 20 Feb 2009 17:42:51 GMT'
246|
247|Because ETags can be weak or strong there are methods to set them:
248|
249|>>> response.etag = "12345-abcd"
250|>>> response.headers['etag']
251|'"12345-abcd"'
252|>>> response.etag
253|<ETag '12345-abcd' strong>
254|>>> response.etag = ETag("12345-abcd", True)
255|>>> response.etag
256|<ETag '12345-abcd' weak>
257|
258|Some headers are available as mutable structures.  For example most
259|of the `Content-` headers are sets of values:
260|
261|>>> response.content_language.add('en-us')
262|>>> response.content_language.add('en')
263|>>> response.headers['Content-Language']
264|'en-us, en'
265|
266|Also here this works in both directions:
267|
268|>>> response.headers['Content-Language'] = 'de-AT, de'
269|>>> response.content_language
270|HeaderSet(['de-AT', 'de'])
271|
272|Authentication headers can be set that way as well:
273|
274|>>> response.www_authenticate.set_basic("My protected resource")
275|>>> response.headers['www-authenticate']
276|'Basic realm="My protected resource"'
277|
278|Cookies can be set as well:
279|
280|>>> response.set_cookie('name', 'value')
281|>>> response.headers['Set-Cookie']
282|'name=value; Path=/'
283|>>> response.set_cookie('name2', 'value2')
284|
285|If headers appear multiple times you can use the :meth:`~Headers.getlist`
286|method to get all values for a header:
287|
288|>>> response.headers.getlist('Set-Cookie')
289|['name=value; Path=/', 'name2=value2; Path=/']
290|
291|If the request has precondition headers, you can make the response conditional
292|to avoid sending data if it's already cached by the client. Ensure that the
293|response has set :attr:`~.Response.etag`, :attr:`~.Response.last_modified`,
294|then call :meth:`~.Response.apply_conditions`.
295|
296|If the request has a ``Range`` header, you can apply the range to the response
297|to send only the partial data requested by the client. Ensure that the response
298|has set :attr:`~.Response.data`, :attr:`~.Response.content_length`,
299|:attr:`~.Response.etag`, and :attr:`~.Response.last_modified`, then call
300|:meth:`~.Response.apply_range`.
301|
302|
303|Trusting Data
304|-------------
305|
306|When parsing request data, Werkzeug will discard values with invalid syntax.
307|However, it may choose to skip invalid values in a list of values, returning the
308|valid ones. Or it may allow through values that are not technically allowed by
309|an HTTP spec, but that don't interfere with the syntax being parsed, such as
310|values that contain characters outside the token set, additional whitespace,
311|ignoring empty values, etc. Werkzeug may become more strict over time, but in
312|general it's not a goal to strictly validate every value.
313|
314|When generating response data, responsibility is placed on the application
315|developers to not pass untrusted user input. Most arguments to most functions
316|are assumed to be trusted and valid. For headers and cookies, Werkzeug will
317|validate or escape _values_, but _keys_ are assumed to be trusted and valid.
318|
319|For web application development in general, never pass untrusted user input
320|without doing your own validation or ensuring that it will be handled safely.
321|For example, use a template engine such as Jinja that escapes HTML characters,
322|use a database ORM such as SQLAlchemy that escapes values in SQL statements, etc.

1|"""
2|X-Forwarded-For Proxy Fix
3|=========================
4|
5|This module provides a middleware that adjusts the WSGI environ based on
6|``X-Forwarded-`` headers that proxies in front of an application may
7|set.
8|
9|It is recommended that the WSGI application and server sit behind a real HTTP
10|server for efficiency and security, and there may be other proxies in front of
11|that depending on the services you use to host the server. In this case, WSGI
12|may see the request as coming from that server rather than the real client.
13|Proxies set various headers to track where the request actually came from.
14|
15|This middleware should only be used if the application is actually
16|behind such a proxy, and should be configured with the number of proxies
17|that are chained in front of it. Not all proxies set all the headers.
18|Since incoming headers can be faked, you must set how many proxies are
19|setting each header so the middleware knows what to trust.
20|
21|If a header has invalid syntax, it is ignored. That is, it will be as if
22|``ProxyFix`` wasn't set for that header, so you'll see the original incorrect
23|but trusted value from the closest proxy.
24|
25|.. autoclass:: ProxyFix
26|
27|:copyright: 2007 Pallets
28|:license: BSD-3-Clause
29|"""
30|
31|from __future__ import annotations
32|
33|import typing as t
34|import wsgiref.types as wt
35|
36|from ..http import parse_list_header
37|
38|
39|class ProxyFix:
40|    """Adjust the WSGI environ based on ``X-Forwarded-`` headers that proxies in
41|    front of the application may set.
42|
43|    -   ``X-Forwarded-For`` sets ``REMOTE_ADDR``.
44|    -   ``X-Forwarded-Proto`` sets ``wsgi.url_scheme``.
45|    -   ``X-Forwarded-Host`` sets ``HTTP_HOST``, ``SERVER_NAME``, and
46|        ``SERVER_PORT``.
47|    -   ``X-Forwarded-Port`` sets ``HTTP_HOST`` and ``SERVER_PORT``.
48|    -   ``X-Forwarded-Prefix`` sets ``SCRIPT_NAME``.
49|
50|    You must tell the middleware how many proxies set each header so it
51|    knows what values to trust. It is a security issue to trust values
52|    that came from the client rather than a proxy.
53|
54|    The original values of the headers are stored in the WSGI
55|    environ as ``werkzeug.proxy_fix.orig``, a dict.
56|
57|    :param app: The WSGI application to wrap.
58|    :param x_for: Number of values to trust for ``X-Forwarded-For``.
59|    :param x_proto: Number of values to trust for ``X-Forwarded-Proto``.
60|    :param x_host: Number of values to trust for ``X-Forwarded-Host``.
61|    :param x_port: Number of values to trust for ``X-Forwarded-Port``.
62|    :param x_prefix: Number of values to trust for
63|        ``X-Forwarded-Prefix``.
64|
65|    .. code-block:: python
66|
67|        from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix import ProxyFix
68|        # App is behind one proxy that sets the -For and -Host headers.
69|        app = ProxyFix(app, x_for=1, x_host=1)
70|
71|    .. versionchanged:: 3.2
72|        ``SERVER_NAME`` and ``SERVER_PORT`` are not modified.
73|
74|    .. versionchanged:: 1.0
75|        The ``num_proxies`` argument and attribute; the ``get_remote_addr`` method; and
76|        the environ keys ``orig_remote_addr``, ``orig_wsgi_url_scheme``, and
77|        ``orig_http_host`` were removed.
78|
79|    .. versionchanged:: 0.15
80|        All headers support multiple values. Each header is configured with a separate
81|        number of trusted proxies.
82|
83|        Original WSGI environ values are stored in the ``werkzeug.proxy_fix.orig`` dict.
84|
85|        Support ``X-Forwarded-Port`` and ``X-Forwarded-Prefix``.
86|
87|        ``X-Forwarded-Host`` and ``X-Forwarded-Port`` modify
88|        ``SERVER_NAME`` and ``SERVER_PORT``.
89|    """
90|
91|    def __init__(
92|        self,
93|        app: wt.WSGIApplication,
94|        x_for: int = 1,
95|        x_proto: int = 1,
96|        x_host: int = 0,
97|        x_port: int = 0,
98|        x_prefix: int = 0,
99|    ) -> None:
100|        self.app = app
101|        self.x_for = x_for
102|        self.x_proto = x_proto
103|        self.x_host = x_host
104|        self.x_port = x_port
105|        self.x_prefix = x_prefix
106|
107|    def _get_real_value(self, trusted: int, value: str | None) -> str | None:
108|        """Get the real value from a list header based on the configured
109|        number of trusted proxies.
110|
111|        :param trusted: Number of values to trust in the header.
112|        :param value: Comma separated list header value to parse.
113|        :return: The real value, or ``None`` if there are fewer values
114|            than the number of trusted proxies.
115|
116|        .. versionchanged:: 1.0
117|            Renamed from ``_get_trusted_comma``.
118|
119|        .. versionadded:: 0.15
120|        """
121|        if not (trusted and value):
122|            return None
123|        values = parse_list_header(value)
124|        if len(values) >= trusted:
125|            return values[-trusted]
126|        return None
127|
128|    def __call__(
129|        self, environ: wt.WSGIEnvironment, start_response: wt.StartResponse
130|    ) -> t.Iterable[bytes]:
131|        """Modify the WSGI environ based on the various ``Forwarded``
132|        headers before calling the wrapped application. Store the
133|        original environ values in ``werkzeug.proxy_fix.orig_{key}``.
134|        """
135|        environ_get = environ.get
136|        environ.update(
137|            {
138|                "werkzeug.proxy_fix.orig": {
139|                    "REMOTE_ADDR": environ_get("REMOTE_ADDR"),
140|                    "wsgi.url_scheme": environ_get("wsgi.url_scheme"),
141|                    "HTTP_HOST": environ_get("HTTP_HOST"),
142|                    "SCRIPT_NAME": environ_get("SCRIPT_NAME"),
143|                }
144|            }
145|        )
146|
147|        if x_for := self._get_real_value(
148|            self.x_for, environ_get("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR")
149|        ):
150|            environ["REMOTE_ADDR"] = x_for
151|
152|        if x_proto := self._get_real_value(
153|            self.x_proto, environ_get("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO")
154|        ):
155|            environ["wsgi.url_scheme"] = x_proto
156|
157|        if x_host := self._get_real_value(
158|            self.x_host, environ_get("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_HOST")
159|        ):
160|            environ["HTTP_HOST"] = x_host
161|
162|        if x_port := self._get_real_value(
163|            self.x_port, environ_get("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PORT")
164|        ):
165|            if host := environ_get("HTTP_HOST"):
166|                # "]" to check for IPv6 address without port
167|                if ":" in host and not host.endswith("]"):
168|                    host = host.rpartition(":")[0]
169|
170|                environ["HTTP_HOST"] = f"{host}:{x_port}"
171|
172|        if x_prefix := self._get_real_value(
173|            self.x_prefix, environ_get("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PREFIX")
174|        ):
175|            environ["SCRIPT_NAME"] = x_prefix
176|
177|        return self.app(environ, start_response)

1|=========================
2|Serving WSGI Applications
3|=========================
4|
5|.. module:: werkzeug.serving
6|
7|There are many ways to serve a WSGI application.  While you're developing it,
8|you usually don't want to have a full-blown webserver like Apache up and
9|running, but instead a simple standalone one.  Because of that Werkzeug comes
10|with a builtin development server.
11|
12|The easiest way is creating a small ``start-myproject.py`` file that runs the
13|application using the builtin server::
14|
15|    from werkzeug.serving import run_simple
16|    from myproject import make_app
17|
18|    app = make_app(...)
19|    run_simple('localhost', 8080, app, use_reloader=True)
20|
21|You can also pass it the `extra_files` keyword argument with a list of
22|additional files (like configuration files) you want to observe.
23|
24|.. autofunction:: run_simple
25|
26|.. autofunction:: is_running_from_reloader
27|
28|.. autofunction:: make_ssl_devcert
29|
30|.. admonition:: Information
31|
32|   The development server is not intended to be used on production systems.
33|   It was designed especially for development purposes and performs poorly
34|   under high load.  For deployment setups have a look at the
35|   :doc:`/deployment/index` pages.
36|
37|.. _reloader:
38|
39|Reloader
40|--------
41|
42|The Werkzeug reloader constantly monitors modules and paths of your web
43|application, and restarts the server if any of the observed files change.
44|
45|There are two backends the reloader supports: ``stat`` and ``watchdog``.
46|
47|- The default ``stat`` backend simply checks the modification time of all files in a
48|  regular interval. This is sufficient for most cases, however, it is known to
49|  drain a laptop's battery.
50|
51|- The ``watchdog`` backend uses filesystem events, and is much faster than
52|  ``stat``. It requires the `watchdog <https://pypi.org/project/watchdog/>`_
53|  module to be installed. The recommended way to achieve this is to add
54|  ``Werkzeug[watchdog]`` to your requirements file.
55|
56|If ``watchdog`` is installed and available it will automatically be used
57|instead of the builtin ``stat`` reloader.
58|
59|To switch between the backends you can use the `reloader_type` parameter of the
60|:func:`run_simple` function. ``'stat'`` sets it to the default stat based
61|polling and ``'watchdog'`` forces it to the watchdog backend.
62|
63|.. note::
64|
65|    Some edge cases, like modules that failed to import correctly, are not
66|    handled by the stat reloader for performance reasons. The watchdog reloader
67|    monitors such files too.
68|
69|
70|Colored Logging
71|---------------
72|
73|The development server highlights the request logs in different colors
74|based on the status code.
75|
76|
77|Virtual Hosts
78|-------------
79|
80|Many web applications utilize multiple subdomains.  This can be a bit tricky
81|to simulate locally.  Fortunately there is the `hosts file`_ that can be used
82|to assign the local computer multiple names.
83|
84|This allows you to call your local computer `yourapplication.local` and
85|`api.yourapplication.local` (or anything else) in addition to `localhost`.
86|
87|You can find the hosts file on the following location:
88|
89|    =============== ==============================================
90|    Windows         ``%SystemRoot%\system32\drivers\etc\hosts``
91|    Linux / OS X    ``/etc/hosts``
92|    =============== ==============================================
93|
94|You can open the file with your favorite text editor and add a new name after
95|`localhost`::
96|
97|    127.0.0.1       localhost yourapplication.local api.yourapplication.local
98|
99|Save the changes and after a while you should be able to access the
100|development server on these host names as well.  You can use the
101|:doc:`/routing` system to dispatch between different hosts or parse
102|:attr:`request.host` yourself.
103|
104|
105|Shutting Down The Server
106|------------------------
107|
108|In some cases it can be useful to shut down a server after handling a
109|request. For example, a local command line tool that needs OAuth
110|authentication could temporarily start a server to listen for a
111|response, record the user's token, then stop the server.
112|
113|One method to do this could be to start a server in a
114|:mod:`multiprocessing` process, then terminate the process after a value
115|is passed back to the parent.
116|
117|.. code-block:: python
118|
119|    import multiprocessing
120|    from werkzeug import Request, Response, run_simple
121|
122|    def get_token(q: multiprocessing.Queue) -> None:
123|        @Request.application
124|        def app(request: Request) -> Response:
125|            q.put(request.args["token"])
126|            return Response("", 204)
127|
128|        run_simple("localhost", 5000, app)
129|
130|    if __name__ == "__main__":
131|        q = multiprocessing.Queue()
132|        p = multiprocessing.Process(target=get_token, args=(q,))
133|        p.start()
134|        print("waiting")
135|        token = q.get(block=True)
136|        p.terminate()
137|        print(token)
138|
139|That example uses Werkzeug's development server, but any production
140|server that can be started as a Python process could use the same
141|technique and should be preferred for security. Another method could be
142|to start a :mod:`subprocess` process and send the value back over
143|``stdout``.
144|
145|
146|Troubleshooting
147|---------------
148|
149|On operating systems that support ipv6 and have it configured such as modern
150|Linux systems, OS X 10.4 or higher as well as Windows Vista some browsers can
151|be painfully slow if accessing your local server.  The reason for this is that
152|sometimes "localhost" is configured to be available on both ipv4 and ipv6 sockets
153|and some browsers will try to access ipv6 first and then ipv4.
154|
155|At the current time the integrated webserver does not support ipv6 and ipv4 at
156|the same time and for better portability ipv4 is the default.
157|
158|If you notice that the web browser takes ages to load the page there are two ways
159|around this issue.  If you don't need ipv6 support you can disable the ipv6 entry
160|in the `hosts file`_ by removing this line::
161|
162|    ::1             localhost
163|
164|Alternatively you can also disable ipv6 support in your browser.  For example
165|if Firefox shows this behavior you can disable it by going to ``about:config``
166|and disabling the `network.dns.disableIPv6` key.  This however is not
167|recommended as of Werkzeug 0.6.1!
168|
169|Starting with Werkzeug 0.6.1, the server will now switch between ipv4 and
170|ipv6 based on your operating system's configuration.  This means if that
171|you disabled ipv6 support in your browser but your operating system is
172|preferring ipv6, you will be unable to connect to your server.  In that
173|situation, you can either remove the localhost entry for ``::1`` or
174|explicitly bind the hostname to an ipv4 address (`127.0.0.1`)
175|
176|.. _hosts file: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosts_file
177|
178|SSL
179|---
180|
181|.. versionadded:: 0.6
182|
183|The builtin server supports SSL for testing purposes.  If an SSL context is
184|provided it will be used.  That means a server can either run in HTTP or HTTPS
185|mode, but not both.
186|
187|Quickstart
188|``````````
189|
190|The easiest way to do SSL based development with Werkzeug is by using it
191|to generate an SSL certificate and private key and storing that somewhere
192|and to then put it there.  For the certificate you need to provide the
193|name of your server on generation or a `CN`.
194|
195|1.  Generate an SSL key and store it somewhere:
196|
197|    >>> from werkzeug.serving import make_ssl_devcert
198|    >>> make_ssl_devcert('/path/to/the/key', host='localhost')
199|    ('/path/to/the/key.crt', '/path/to/the/key.key')
200|
201|2.  Now this tuple can be passed as ``ssl_context`` to the
202|    :func:`run_simple` method::
203|
204|        run_simple('localhost', 4000, application,
205|                   ssl_context=('/path/to/the/key.crt',
206|                                '/path/to/the/key.key'))
207|
208|You will have to acknowledge the certificate in your browser once then.
209|
210|Loading Contexts by Hand
211|````````````````````````
212|
213|You can use a ``ssl.SSLContext`` object instead of a tuple for full
214|control over the TLS configuration.
215|
216|.. code-block:: python
217|
218|    import ssl
219|    ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
220|    ctx.load_cert_chain('ssl.cert', 'ssl.key')
221|    run_simple('localhost', 4000, application, ssl_context=ctx)
222|
223|
224|.. versionchanged 0.10:: ``OpenSSL`` contexts are not supported anymore.
225|
226|Generating Certificates
227|```````````````````````
228|
229|A key and certificate can be created in advance using the openssl tool
230|instead of the :func:`make_ssl_devcert`.  This requires that you have
231|the `openssl` command installed on your system::
232|
233|    $ openssl genrsa 1024 > ssl.key
234|    $ openssl req -new -x509 -nodes -sha1 -days 365 -key ssl.key > ssl.cert
235|
236|Adhoc Certificates
237|``````````````````
238|
239|The easiest way to enable SSL is to start the server in adhoc-mode.  In
240|that case Werkzeug will generate an SSL certificate for you::
241|
242|    run_simple('localhost', 4000, application,
243|               ssl_context='adhoc')
244|
245|The downside of this of course is that you will have to acknowledge the
246|certificate each time the server is reloaded.  Adhoc certificates are
247|discouraged because modern browsers do a bad job at supporting them for
248|security reasons.
249|
250|This feature requires the cryptography library to be installed.
251|
252|
253|Unix Sockets
254|------------
255|
256|The dev server can bind to a Unix socket instead of a TCP socket.
257|:func:`run_simple` will bind to a Unix socket if the ``hostname``
258|parameter starts with ``'unix://'``. ::
259|
260|    from werkzeug.serving import run_simple
261|    run_simple('unix://example.sock', 0, app)

1|"""
2|Application Profiler
3|====================
4|
5|This module provides a middleware that profiles each request with the
6|:mod:`cProfile` module. This can help identify bottlenecks in your code
7|that may be slowing down your application.
8|
9|.. autoclass:: ProfilerMiddleware
10|
11|:copyright: 2007 Pallets
12|:license: BSD-3-Clause
13|"""
14|
15|from __future__ import annotations
16|
17|import os.path
18|import sys
19|import time
20|import typing as t
21|import wsgiref.types as wt
22|from pstats import Stats
23|from types import TracebackType
24|
25|if sys.version_info >= (3, 15):
26|    from profiling.tracing import Profile
27|else:
28|    try:
29|        from cProfile import Profile
30|    except ImportError:
31|        from profile import Profile  # type: ignore[assignment]
32|
33|
34|class ProfilerMiddleware:
35|    """Wrap a WSGI application and profile the execution of each
36|    request. Responses are buffered so that timings are more exact.
37|
38|    If ``stream`` is given, :class:`pstats.Stats` are written to it
39|    after each request. If ``profile_dir`` is given, :mod:`cProfile`
40|    data files are saved to that directory, one file per request.
41|
42|    The filename can be customized by passing ``filename_format``. If
43|    it is a string, it will be formatted using :meth:`str.format` with
44|    the following fields available:
45|
46|    -   ``{method}`` - The request method; GET, POST, etc.
47|    -   ``{path}`` - The request path or 'root' should one not exist.
48|    -   ``{elapsed}`` - The elapsed time of the request in milliseconds.
49|    -   ``{time}`` - The time of the request.
50|
51|    If it is a callable, it will be called with the WSGI ``environ`` and
52|    be expected to return a filename string. The ``environ`` dictionary
53|    will also have the ``"werkzeug.profiler"`` key populated with a
54|    dictionary containing the following fields (more may be added in the
55|    future):
56|    -   ``{elapsed}`` - The elapsed time of the request in milliseconds.
57|    -   ``{time}`` - The time of the request.
58|
59|    :param app: The WSGI application to wrap.
60|    :param stream: Write stats to this stream. Disable with ``None``.
61|    :param sort_by: A tuple of columns to sort stats by. See
62|        :meth:`pstats.Stats.sort_stats`.
63|    :param restrictions: A tuple of restrictions to filter stats by. See
64|        :meth:`pstats.Stats.print_stats`.
65|    :param profile_dir: Save profile data files to this directory.
66|    :param filename_format: Format string for profile data file names,
67|        or a callable returning a name. See explanation above.
68|
69|    .. code-block:: python
70|
71|        from werkzeug.middleware.profiler import ProfilerMiddleware
72|        app = ProfilerMiddleware(app)
73|
74|    .. versionchanged:: 3.0
75|        Added the ``"werkzeug.profiler"`` key to the ``filename_format(environ)``
76|        parameter with the  ``elapsed`` and ``time`` fields.
77|
78|    .. versionchanged:: 0.15
79|        Stats are written even if ``profile_dir`` is given, and can be
80|        disable by passing ``stream=None``.
81|
82|    .. versionadded:: 0.15
83|        Added ``filename_format``.
84|
85|    .. versionadded:: 0.9
86|        Added ``restrictions`` and ``profile_dir``.
87|    """
88|
89|    def __init__(
90|        self,
91|        app: wt.WSGIApplication,
92|        stream: t.IO[str] | None = sys.stdout,
93|        sort_by: t.Iterable[str] = ("time", "calls"),
94|        restrictions: t.Iterable[str | int | float] = (),
95|        profile_dir: str | None = None,
96|        filename_format: str = "{method}.{path}.{elapsed:.0f}ms.{time:.0f}.prof",
97|    ) -> None:
98|        self._app = app
99|        self._stream = stream
100|        self._sort_by = sort_by
101|        self._restrictions = restrictions
102|        self._profile_dir = profile_dir
103|        self._filename_format = filename_format
104|
105|    def __call__(
106|        self, environ: wt.WSGIEnvironment, start_response: wt.StartResponse
107|    ) -> t.Iterable[bytes]:
108|        response_body: list[bytes] = []
109|
110|        def catching_start_response(
111|            status: str,
112|            headers: list[tuple[str, str]],
113|            exc_info: tuple[type[BaseException], BaseException, TracebackType]
114|            | tuple[None, None, None]
115|            | None = None,
116|        ) -> t.Callable[[bytes], object]:
117|            start_response(status, headers, exc_info)
118|            return response_body.append
119|
120|        def runapp() -> None:
121|            app_iter = self._app(
122|                environ, t.cast(wt.StartResponse, catching_start_response)
123|            )
124|            response_body.extend(app_iter)
125|
126|            if hasattr(app_iter, "close"):
127|                app_iter.close()
128|
129|        profile = Profile()
130|        start = time.time()
131|        profile.runcall(runapp)
132|        body = b"".join(response_body)
133|        elapsed = time.time() - start
134|
135|        if self._profile_dir is not None:
136|            if callable(self._filename_format):
137|                environ["werkzeug.profiler"] = {
138|                    "elapsed": elapsed * 1000.0,
139|                    "time": time.time(),
140|                }
141|                filename = self._filename_format(environ)
142|            else:
143|                filename = self._filename_format.format(
144|                    method=environ["REQUEST_METHOD"],
145|                    path=environ["PATH_INFO"].strip("/").replace("/", ".") or "root",
146|                    elapsed=elapsed * 1000.0,
147|                    time=time.time(),
148|                )
149|            filename = os.path.join(self._profile_dir, filename)
150|            profile.dump_stats(filename)
151|
152|        if self._stream is not None:
153|            stats = Stats(profile, stream=self._stream)
154|            stats.sort_stats(*self._sort_by)
155|            print("-" * 80, file=self._stream)
156|            path_info = environ.get("PATH_INFO", "")
157|            print(f"PATH: {path_info!r}", file=self._stream)
158|            stats.print_stats(*self._restrictions)
159|            print(f"{'-' * 80}\n", file=self._stream)
160|
161|        return [body]

1|"""
2|Application Dispatcher
3|======================
4|
5|This middleware creates a single WSGI application that dispatches to
6|multiple other WSGI applications mounted at different URL paths.
7|
8|A common example is writing a Single Page Application, where you have a
9|backend API and a frontend written in JavaScript that does the routing
10|in the browser rather than requesting different pages from the server.
11|The frontend is a single HTML and JS file that should be served for any
12|path besides "/api".
13|
14|This example dispatches to an API app under "/api", an admin app
15|under "/admin", and an app that serves frontend files for all other
16|requests::
17|
18|    app = DispatcherMiddleware(serve_frontend, {
19|        '/api': api_app,
20|        '/admin': admin_app,
21|    })
22|
23|In production, you might instead handle this at the HTTP server level,
24|serving files or proxying to application servers based on location. The
25|API and admin apps would each be deployed with a separate WSGI server,
26|and the static files would be served directly by the HTTP server.
27|
28|.. autoclass:: DispatcherMiddleware
29|
30|:copyright: 2007 Pallets
31|:license: BSD-3-Clause
32|"""
33|
34|from __future__ import annotations
35|
36|import typing as t
37|import wsgiref.types as wt
38|
39|
40|class DispatcherMiddleware:
41|    """Combine multiple applications as a single WSGI application.
42|    Requests are dispatched to an application based on the path it is
43|    mounted under.
44|
45|    :param app: The WSGI application to dispatch to if the request
46|        doesn't match a mounted path.
47|    :param mounts: Maps path prefixes to applications for dispatching.
48|    """
49|
50|    def __init__(
51|        self,
52|        app: wt.WSGIApplication,
53|        mounts: dict[str, wt.WSGIApplication] | None = None,
54|    ) -> None:
55|        self.app = app
56|        self.mounts = mounts or {}
57|
58|    def __call__(
59|        self, environ: wt.WSGIEnvironment, start_response: wt.StartResponse
60|    ) -> t.Iterable[bytes]:
61|        script = environ.get("PATH_INFO", "")
62|        path_info = ""
63|
64|        while "/" in script:
65|            if script in self.mounts:
66|                app = self.mounts[script]
67|                break
68|
69|            script, last_item = script.rsplit("/", 1)
70|            path_info = f"/{last_item}{path_info}"
71|        else:
72|            app = self.mounts.get(script, self.app)
73|
74|        original_script_name = environ.get("SCRIPT_NAME", "")
75|        environ["SCRIPT_NAME"] = original_script_name + script
76|        environ["PATH_INFO"] = path_info
77|        return app(environ, start_response)
