--- FILE: docs/request_data.rst ---
1|Reading and Parsing Request Data
2|================================
3|
4|Werkzeug's :class:`.Request` class provides ways to read and parse the data sent
5|in a request.
6|
7|-   :attr:`.Request.form` and :attr:`.Request.files` will consume and parse the
8|    stream as HTML form data if the content type is
9|    ``application/x-www-form-urlencoded`` or ``multipart/form-data``.
10|-   :attr:`.Request.json` and :meth:`.Request.get_json` will consume and parse
11|    the stream as JSON if the content type is ``application/json``.
12|-   :attr:`.Request.data` and :attr:`.Request.get_data` will consume the stream
13|    and return the raw bytes. However, ``data`` will be empty if it was actually
14|    form data, and ``form`` and ``files`` will be populated instead.
15|
16|All of these read from :attr:`.Request.stream`, which can only be consumed once.
17|However, all of these cache their data by default, so they can be accessed
18|multiple times even though the stream remains consumed.
19|
20|If you access these then try to read ``stream``, it will be empty. If you read
21|from ``stream`` before accessing these, they will only see the remaining data,
22|and then ``stream`` will be empty.
23|
24|If your application handles request data other than HTML forms or JSON, you can
25|subclass :class:`.Request` and add your own properties or methods that read and
26|parse ``stream``.
27|
28|
29|Limiting Request Data
30|---------------------
31|
32|The :class:`Request` class provides a few attributes to control how much data is
33|processed from the request body. This can help mitigate DoS attacks that craft
34|the request in such a way that the server uses too many resources to handle it.
35|Each of these limits will raise a :exc:`.RequestEntityTooLarge` if they are
36|exceeded.
37|
38|-   :attr:`~Request.max_content_length` - Stop reading data after this many
39|    bytes. This amount of memory, plus additional object overhead, could be used
40|    during one request. It's better to configure this in the WSGI server or HTTP
41|    server, rather than the WSGI application, which is why it's not set by
42|    default. Not setting it anywhere would be an issue with that application,
43|    not with Werkzeug.
44|-   :attr:`~Request.max_form_memory_size` - Stop parsing ``multipart/form-data``
45|    if any non-file part is larger than this number of bytes. File parts can
46|    be larger, they are moved to disk at this limit. The default is 500kB. This
47|    is an additional check, it does not replace ``max_content_length``.
48|-   :attr:`~Request.max_form_parts` - Stop parsing ``multipart/form-data`` if
49|    more than this number of parts are received. This is useful to stop a very
50|    large number of very small fields, especially files. The default is 1000.
51|    This is an additional check, it does not replace ``max_content_length``.
52|
53|Each of these values can be set on the ``Request`` class to affect the default
54|for all requests, or on a ``request`` instance to change the behavior for a
55|specific request. For example, a small limit can be set by default, and a large
56|limit can be set on an endpoint that accepts video uploads. These values should
57|be tuned to the specific needs of your application and endpoints.
58|
59|Using Werkzeug to set these limits is only one layer of protection. WSGI servers
60|and HTTPS servers should set their own limits on size and timeouts. The
61|operating system or container manager should set limits on memory and processing
62|time for server processes.
63|
64|If a 413 Content Too Large error is returned before the entire request is read,
65|clients may show a "connection reset" failure instead of the 413 error. This is
66|based on how the WSGI/HTTP server and client handle connections, it's not
67|something the WSGI application (Werkzeug) has control over.
68|
69|
70|WSGI Server Input Termination
71|-----------------------------
72|
73|The raw WSGI input stream (``environ["wsgi.input"]``) is not safe to read
74|directly for a number of reasons. While not part of the WSGI spec, it is widely
75|accepted that the WSGI server should handle waiting for available data,
76|buffering, and detect EOF or end of chunked input to terminate the stream. The
77|WSGI server indicates that it does this by setting
78|``environ["wsgi.input_terminated"] = True``. Otherwise, Werkzeug will only
79|allow reading the stream if ``Content-Length`` is set.
80|
81|If the WSGI server sets ``wsgi.input_terminated``, this does not mean that the
82|stream is not infinite, only that it will be properly buffered and terminated if
83|it does end. Therefore, you must set limits as described above, or otherwise
84|be prepared to handle infinite streams.
85|
86|
87|Reading the Stream in Middleware
88|--------------------------------
89|
90|When writing WSGI middleware, it is important to remember that the input stream
91|can only be read once. If middleware reads it, it will not be available to the
92|application.
93|
94|Most middleware should not need to read the stream. In rare cases where it does,
95|you can replace the stream with what you've read to avoid this in some cases.
96|
97|.. code-block:: python
98|
99|    environ["wsgi.input"] = BytesIO(request.data)
100|    return wrapped_app(environ, start_response)
101|
102|However, this will cause the entire stream to be stored in memory for the
103|remainder of the request. Therefore it will also not work for infinite streams.
--- END FILE: docs/request_data.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/debug.rst ---
1|Debugging Applications
2|======================
3|
4|.. module:: werkzeug.debug
5|
6|Depending on the WSGI gateway/server, exceptions are handled
7|differently. Most of the time, exceptions go to stderr or the error log,
8|and a generic "500 Internal Server Error" message is displayed.
9|
10|Since this is not the best debugging environment, Werkzeug provides a
11|WSGI middleware that renders nice tracebacks, optionally with an
12|interactive debug console to execute code in any frame.
13|
14|.. danger::
15|
16|    The debugger allows the execution of arbitrary code which makes it a
17|    major security risk. **The debugger must never be used on production
18|    machines. We cannot stress this enough. Do not enable the debugger
19|    in production.** Production means anything that is not development,
20|    and anything that is publicly accessible.
21|
22|.. note::
23|
24|    The interactive debugger does not work in forking environments, such
25|    as a server that starts multiple processes. Most such environments
26|    are production servers, where the debugger should not be enabled
27|    anyway.
28|
29|
30|Enabling the Debugger
31|---------------------
32|
33|Enable the debugger by wrapping the application with the
34|:class:`DebuggedApplication` middleware. Alternatively, you can pass
35|``use_debugger=True`` to :func:`run_simple` and it will do that for you.
36|
37|.. autoclass:: DebuggedApplication
38|
39|
40|Using the Debugger
41|------------------
42|
43|Once enabled and an error happens during a request you will see a
44|detailed traceback instead of a generic "internal server error". The
45|traceback is still output to the terminal as well.
46|
47|The error message is displayed at the top. Clicking it jumps to the
48|bottom of the traceback. Frames that represent user code, as opposed to
49|built-ins or installed packages, are highlighted blue. Clicking a
50|frame will show more lines for context, clicking again will hide them.
51|
52|If you have the ``evalex`` feature enabled you can get a console for
53|every frame in the traceback by hovering over a frame and clicking the
54|console icon that appears at the right. Once clicked a console opens
55|where you can execute Python code in:
56|
57|.. image:: _static/debug-screenshot.png
58|   :alt: a screenshot of the interactive debugger
59|   :align: center
60|
61|Inside the interactive consoles you can execute any kind of Python code.
62|Unlike regular Python consoles the output of the object reprs is colored
63|and stripped to a reasonable size by default. If the output is longer
64|than what the console decides to display a small plus sign is added to
65|the repr and a click will expand the repr.
66|
67|To display all variables that are defined in the current frame you can
68|use the ``dump()`` function. You can call it without arguments to get a
69|detailed list of all variables and their values, or with an object as
70|argument to get a detailed list of all the attributes it has.
71|
72|
73|Debugger PIN
74|------------
75|
76|The debug console is protected by a PIN. This is a security helper to make it
77|less likely for the debugger to be exploited if you forget to disable it when
78|deploying to production. The PIN based authentication is enabled by default.
79|
80|The first time a console is opened, a dialog will prompt for a PIN that
81|is printed to the command line. The PIN is generated in a stable way
82|that is specific to the project. An explicit PIN can be provided through
83|the environment variable ``WERKZEUG_DEBUG_PIN``. This can be set to a
84|number and will become the PIN. This variable can also be set to the
85|value ``off`` to disable the PIN check entirely.
86|
87|If an incorrect PIN is entered too many times the server needs to be
88|restarted.
89|
90|**This feature is not meant to entirely secure the debugger. It is
91|intended to make it harder for an attacker to exploit the debugger.
92|Never enable the debugger in production.**
93|
94|
95|Allowed Hosts
96|-------------
97|
98|The debug console will only be served if the request comes from a trusted host.
99|If a request comes from a browser page that is not served on a trusted URL, a
100|400 error will be returned.
101|
102|By default, ``localhost``, any ``.localhost`` subdomain, and ``127.0.0.1`` are
103|trusted. ``run_simple`` will trust its ``hostname`` argument as well. To change
104|this further, use the debug middleware directly rather than through
105|``use_debugger=True``.
106|
107|.. code-block:: python
108|
109|    if os.environ.get("USE_DEBUGGER") in {"1", "true"}:
110|        app = DebuggedApplication(app, evalex=True)
111|        app.trusted_hosts = [...]
112|
113|    run_simple("localhost", 8080, app)
114|
115|**This feature is not meant to entirely secure the debugger. It is
116|intended to make it harder for an attacker to exploit the debugger.
117|Never enable the debugger in production.**
118|
119|
120|Pasting Errors
121|--------------
122|
123|If you click on the "Traceback (most recent call last)" header, the
124|view switches to a traditional text-based traceback. You can copy and
125|paste this in order to provide information when asking a question or
126|reporting an issue.
--- END FILE: docs/debug.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/wrappers.rst ---
1|Request and Response Objects
2|============================
3|
4|The :class:`.Request` and :class:`.Response` classes are wrappers around the
5|WSGI request data and response building interface.
6|
7|The :class:`.Request` class wraps the incoming WSGI ``environ`` and provides
8|methods to parse the headers and form data. All parsing is cached, so everything
9|can be accessed multiple times efficiently. This is not thread-safe, so use a
10|lock if you'll access a request's data from multiple threads. It's not possible
11|to pickle or send it to other processes.
12|
13|The request data comes from the client and the server, it's not something that
14|makes sense to change within the application. Werkzeug tries to prevent mutation
15|where it can, but in general you should not modify the request.
16|
17|The :class:`.Response` class provides an interface for building the WSGI
18|response data. Many of its attributes are header properties, which allow working
19|with the headers as Python types rather than raw strings. Set the attribute to
20|an instance of the type to set the header. If the type is a dict or
21|:doc:`datastructure <datastructures>`, modifying it will update the header,
22|although this will be less efficient compared to setting a new instance if you
23|modify it multiple times. Set it to ``None`` or use ``del`` to unset the header.
24|Each property below documents its type and what behaviors it has.
25|
26|
27|Wrapping a WSGI Application
28|---------------------------
29|
30|A WSGI application is a Python function that takes two arguments from the server,
31|``environ``, and ``start_response``. ``environ`` contains the incoming request
32|data. To return a response, the function calls ``start_response(status, headers)``,
33|then returns an iterator of bytes as the body.
34|
35|.. code-block:: python
36|
37|    def application(
38|        environ: dict[str, Any],
39|        start_response: Callable[[str, list[tuple[str, str]]], None]
40|    ) -> Iterator[bytes]:
41|        start_response("200 OK", [])
42|        return [b"Hello, World!"]
43|
44|This is missing a lot. It's not sending any headers, including basic things
45|such as ``Content-Length``. It would have to parse out values from ``environ``
46|to do something basic like getting a ``?name=Python`` value from the URL. You
47|have to encode the body to bytes even for text data.
48|
49|You can wrap ``environ`` with :class:`.Request`, and use :class:`.Response` to
50|build the status, headers, and body.
51|
52|.. code-block:: python
53|
54|    from werkzeug import Request, Response
55|
56|    def application(environ, start_response):
57|        request = Request(environ)
58|        response = Response(f"Hello, {request.args.get("name", "World")}!")
59|        return response(environ, start_response)
60|
61|This can be simplified even further with the :meth:`.Request.application`
62|decorator. Now your function will be passed a :class:`.Request`, and will return
63|a :class:`.Response`. It can also raise Werkzeug's :doc:`exceptions` which will
64|be converted to responses.
65|
66|.. code-block:: python
67|
68|    from werkzeug import Request, Response
69|
70|    @Request.application
71|    def application(request: Request) -> Response:
72|        return Response(f"Hello, {request.args.get("name", "World")}!")
73|
74|API
75|---
76|
77|.. module:: werkzeug.wrappers
78|
79|.. autoclass:: Request
80|    :members:
81|    :inherited-members:
82|
83|    .. automethod:: _get_file_stream
84|
85|.. autoclass:: Response
86|    :members:
87|    :inherited-members:
88|
89|    .. automethod:: __call__
90|
91|    .. automethod:: _ensure_sequence
92|
93|
94|Reusing or Caching Response Objects
95|-----------------------------------
96|
97|Whatever you cache, be sure it's keyed accurately based what the data or
98|response depends on.
99|
100|An arbitrary :class:`.Response` cannot be guaranteed to be reusable, copyable,
101|or pickleable for caching.
102|
103|-   If the response is based on the current request, such as a current user,
104|    preconditions, ranges, etc., it's only useful to reuse for identical
105|    requests.
106|-   Any change to an in-memory shared response will affect every subsequent use.
107|-   If the response is a generator, buffering it defeats the purpose of making
108|    it a streaming response to begin with, and can use a large amount of memory.
109|-   Any :meth:`call_on_close` callbacks are kept. They will still be called on
110|    every use of the response, and could refer to resources that are no longer
111|    available in the next request context. They can also hold references that
112|    prevent old objects from being garbage collected.
113|
114|Prefer caching the processes that produced the response, such as querying a
115|database, calculating a value, or rendering a template. Then building a fresh
116|response object from that cached data will be quick without running into these
117|issues.
118|
119|If you really need to share a response object, ensure it is not dependent on the
120|current request, is not subsequently mutated, is a fixed-length sequence, and
121|does not have any callbacks.
--- END FILE: docs/wrappers.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/deployment/uwsgi.rst ---
1|uWSGI
2|=====
3|
4|`uWSGI`_ is a fast, compiled server suite with extensive configuration
5|and capabilities beyond a basic server.
6|
7|*   It can be very performant due to being a compiled program.
8|*   It is complex to configure beyond the basic application, and has so
9|    many options that it can be difficult for beginners to understand.
10|*   It does not support Windows (but does run on WSL).
11|*   It requires a compiler to install in some cases.
12|
13|This page outlines the basics of running uWSGI. Be sure to read its
14|documentation to understand what features are available.
15|
16|.. _uWSGI: https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
17|
18|
19|Installing
20|----------
21|
22|uWSGI has multiple ways to install it. The most straightforward is to
23|install the ``pyuwsgi`` package, which provides precompiled wheels for
24|common platforms. However, it does not provide SSL support, which can be
25|provided with a reverse proxy instead.
26|
27|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install ``pyuwsgi``.
28|
29|.. code-block:: text
30|
31|    $ cd hello-app
32|    $ python -m venv venv
33|    $ . venv/bin/activate
34|    $ pip install .  # install your application
35|    $ pip install pyuwsgi
36|
37|If you have a compiler available, you can install the ``uwsgi`` package
38|instead. Or install the ``pyuwsgi`` package from sdist instead of wheel.
39|Either method will include SSL support.
40|
41|.. code-block:: text
42|
43|    $ pip install uwsgi
44|
45|    # or
46|    $ pip install --no-binary pyuwsgi pyuwsgi
47|
48|
49|Running
50|-------
51|
52|The most basic way to run uWSGI is to tell it to start an HTTP server
53|and import your application.
54|
55|.. code-block:: text
56|
57|    $ uwsgi --http 127.0.0.1:8000 --master -p 4 -w hello:app
58|
59|    *** Starting uWSGI 2.0.20 (64bit) on [x] ***
60|    *** Operational MODE: preforking ***
61|    mounting hello:app on /
62|    spawned uWSGI master process (pid: x)
63|    spawned uWSGI worker 1 (pid: x, cores: 1)
64|    spawned uWSGI worker 2 (pid: x, cores: 1)
65|    spawned uWSGI worker 3 (pid: x, cores: 1)
66|    spawned uWSGI worker 4 (pid: x, cores: 1)
67|    spawned uWSGI http 1 (pid: x)
68|
69|If you're using the app factory pattern, you'll need to create a small
70|Python file to create the app, then point uWSGI at that.
71|
72|.. code-block:: python
73|    :caption: ``wsgi.py``
74|
75|    from hello import create_app
76|
77|    app = create_app()
78|
79|.. code-block:: text
80|
81|    $ uwsgi --http 127.0.0.1:8000 --master -p 4 -w wsgi:app
82|
83|The ``--http`` option starts an HTTP server at 127.0.0.1 port 8000. The
84|``--master`` option specifies the standard worker manager. The ``-p``
85|option starts 4 worker processes; a starting value could be ``CPU * 2``.
86|The ``-w`` option tells uWSGI how to import your application
87|
88|
89|Binding Externally
90|------------------
91|
92|uWSGI should not be run as root with the configuration shown in this doc
93|because it would cause your application code to run as root, which is
94|not secure. However, this means it will not be possible to bind to port
95|80 or 443. Instead, a reverse proxy such as :doc:`nginx` or
96|:doc:`apache-httpd` should be used in front of uWSGI. It is possible to
97|run uWSGI as root securely, but that is beyond the scope of this doc.
98|
99|uWSGI has optimized integration with `Nginx uWSGI`_ and
100|`Apache mod_proxy_uwsgi`_, and possibly other servers, instead of using
101|a standard HTTP proxy. That configuration is beyond the scope of this
102|doc, see the links for more information.
103|
104|.. _Nginx uWSGI: https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Nginx.html
105|.. _Apache mod_proxy_uwsgi: https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Apache.html#mod-proxy-uwsgi
106|
107|You can bind to all external IPs on a non-privileged port using the
108|``--http 0.0.0.0:8000`` option. Don't do this when using a reverse proxy
109|setup, otherwise it will be possible to bypass the proxy.
110|
111|.. code-block:: text
112|
113|    $ uwsgi --http 0.0.0.0:8000 --master -p 4 -w wsgi:app
114|
115|``0.0.0.0`` is not a valid address to navigate to, you'd use a specific
116|IP address in your browser.
117|
118|
119|Async with gevent
120|-----------------
121|
122|The default sync worker is appropriate for many use cases. If you need
123|asynchronous support, uWSGI provides a `gevent`_ worker. This is not the
124|same as Python's ``async/await``, or the ASGI server spec. You must
125|actually use gevent in your own code to see any benefit to using the
126|worker.
127|
128|When using gevent, greenlet>=1.0 is required, otherwise context locals
129|such as ``request`` will not work as expected. When using PyPy,
130|PyPy>=7.3.7 is required.
131|
132|.. code-block:: text
133|
134|    $ uwsgi --http 127.0.0.1:8000 --master --gevent 100 -w wsgi:app
135|
136|    *** Starting uWSGI 2.0.20 (64bit) on [x] ***
137|    *** Operational MODE: async ***
138|    mounting hello:app on /
139|    spawned uWSGI master process (pid: x)
140|    spawned uWSGI worker 1 (pid: x, cores: 100)
141|    spawned uWSGI http 1 (pid: x)
142|    *** running gevent loop engine [addr:x] ***
143|
144|
145|.. _gevent: https://www.gevent.org/
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/uwsgi.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/deployment/gunicorn.rst ---
1|Gunicorn
2|========
3|
4|`Gunicorn`_ is a pure Python WSGI server with simple configuration and
5|multiple worker implementations for performance tuning.
6|
7|*   It tends to integrate easily with hosting platforms.
8|*   It does not support Windows (but does run on WSL).
9|*   It is easy to install as it does not require additional dependencies
10|    or compilation.
11|*   It has built-in async worker support using gevent or eventlet.
12|
13|This page outlines the basics of running Gunicorn. Be sure to read its
14|`documentation`_ and use ``gunicorn --help`` to understand what features
15|are available.
16|
17|.. _Gunicorn: https://gunicorn.org/
18|.. _documentation: https://docs.gunicorn.org/
19|
20|
21|Installing
22|----------
23|
24|Gunicorn is easy to install, as it does not require external
25|dependencies or compilation. It runs on Windows only under WSL.
26|
27|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install
28|``gunicorn``.
29|
30|.. code-block:: text
31|
32|    $ cd hello-app
33|    $ python -m venv venv
34|    $ . venv/bin/activate
35|    $ pip install .  # install your application
36|    $ pip install gunicorn
37|
38|
39|Running
40|-------
41|
42|The only required argument to Gunicorn tells it how to load your
43|application. The syntax is ``{module_import}:{app_variable}``.
44|``module_import`` is the dotted import name to the module with your
45|application. ``app_variable`` is the variable with the application. It
46|can also be a function call (with any arguments) if you're using the
47|app factory pattern.
48|
49|.. code-block:: text
50|
51|    # equivalent to 'from hello import app'
52|    $ gunicorn -w 4 'hello:app'
53|
54|    # equivalent to 'from hello import create_app; create_app()'
55|    $ gunicorn -w 4 'hello:create_app()'
56|
57|    Starting gunicorn 20.1.0
58|    Listening at: http://127.0.0.1:8000 (x)
59|    Using worker: sync
60|    Booting worker with pid: x
61|    Booting worker with pid: x
62|    Booting worker with pid: x
63|    Booting worker with pid: x
64|
65|The ``-w`` option specifies the number of processes to run; a starting
66|value could be ``CPU * 2``. The default is only 1 worker, which is
67|probably not what you want for the default worker type.
68|
69|Logs for each request aren't shown by default, only worker info and
70|errors are shown. To show access logs on stdout, use the
71|``--access-logfile=-`` option.
72|
73|
74|Binding Externally
75|------------------
76|
77|Gunicorn should not be run as root because it would cause your
78|application code to run as root, which is not secure. However, this
79|means it will not be possible to bind to port 80 or 443. Instead, a
80|reverse proxy such as :doc:`nginx` or :doc:`apache-httpd` should be used
81|in front of Gunicorn.
82|
83|You can bind to all external IPs on a non-privileged port using the
84|``-b 0.0.0.0`` option. Don't do this when using a reverse proxy setup,
85|otherwise it will be possible to bypass the proxy.
86|
87|.. code-block:: text
88|
89|    $ gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0 'hello:create_app()'
90|    Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000 (x)
91|
92|``0.0.0.0`` is not a valid address to navigate to, you'd use a specific
93|IP address in your browser.
94|
95|
96|Async with gevent or eventlet
97|-----------------------------
98|
99|The default sync worker is appropriate for many use cases. If you need
100|asynchronous support, Gunicorn provides workers using either `gevent`_
101|or `eventlet`_. This is not the same as Python's ``async/await``, or the
102|ASGI server spec. You must actually use gevent/eventlet in your own code
103|to see any benefit to using the workers.
104|
105|When using either gevent or eventlet, greenlet>=1.0 is required,
106|otherwise context locals such as ``request`` will not work as expected.
107|When using PyPy, PyPy>=7.3.7 is required.
108|
109|To use gevent:
110|
111|.. code-block:: text
112|
113|    $ gunicorn -k gevent 'hello:create_app()'
114|    Starting gunicorn 20.1.0
115|    Listening at: http://127.0.0.1:8000 (x)
116|    Using worker: gevent
117|    Booting worker with pid: x
118|
119|To use eventlet:
120|
121|.. code-block:: text
122|
123|    $ gunicorn -k eventlet 'hello:create_app()'
124|    Starting gunicorn 20.1.0
125|    Listening at: http://127.0.0.1:8000 (x)
126|    Using worker: eventlet
127|    Booting worker with pid: x
128|
129|.. _gevent: https://www.gevent.org/
130|.. _eventlet: https://eventlet.net/
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/gunicorn.rst ---

2|HTTP Utilities
3|==============
4|

6|

12|
13|Datetime Functions
14|==================
15|
16|These functions simplify working with times in an HTTP context. Werkzeug
17|produces timezone-aware :class:`~datetime.datetime` objects in UTC. When
18|passing datetime objects to Werkzeug, it assumes any naive datetime is
19|in UTC.
20|
21|When comparing datetime values from Werkzeug, your own datetime objects
22|must also be timezone-aware, or you must make the values from Werkzeug
23|naive.
24|
25|*   ``dt = datetime.now(timezone.utc)`` gets the current time in UTC.
26|*   ``dt = datetime(..., tzinfo=timezone.utc)`` creates a time in UTC.
27|*   ``dt = dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`` makes a naive object aware
28|    by assuming it's in UTC.
29|*   ``dt = dt.replace(tzinfo=None)`` makes an aware object naive.

--- FILE: docs/local.rst ---
1|Context Locals
2|==============
3|
4|.. module:: werkzeug.local
5|
6|You may find that you have some data during each request that you want
7|to use across functions. Instead of passing these as arguments between
8|every function, you may want to access them as global data. However,
9|using global variables in Python web applications is not thread safe;
10|different workers might interfere with each others' data.
11|
12|Instead of storing common data during a request using global variables,
13|you must use context-local variables instead. A context local is
14|defined/imported globally, but the data it contains is specific to the
15|current thread, asyncio task, or greenlet. You won't accidentally get
16|or overwrite another worker's data.
17|
18|The current approach for storing per-context data in Python is the
19|:class:`contextvars` module. Context vars store data per thread, async
20|task, or greenlet. This replaces the older :class:`threading.local`
21|which only handled threads.
22|
23|Werkzeug provides wrappers around :class:`~contextvars.ContextVar` to
24|make it easier to work with.
25|
26|
27|Proxy Objects
28|=============
29|
30|:class:`LocalProxy` allows treating a context var as an object directly
31|instead of needing to use and check
32|:meth:`ContextVar.get() <contextvars.ContextVar.get>`. If the context
33|var is set, the local proxy will look and behave like the object the var
34|is set to. If it's not set, a ``RuntimeError`` is raised for most
35|operations.
36|
37|.. code-block:: python
38|
39|    from contextvars import ContextVar
40|    from werkzeug.local import LocalProxy
41|
42|    _request_var = ContextVar("request")
43|    request = LocalProxy(_request_var)
44|
45|    from werkzeug.wrappers import Request
46|
47|    @Request.application
48|    def app(r):
49|        _request_var.set(r)
50|        check_auth()
51|        ...
52|
53|    from werkzeug.exceptions import Unauthorized
54|
55|    def check_auth():
56|        if request.form["username"] != "admin":
57|            raise Unauthorized()
58|
59|Accessing ``request`` will point to the specific request that each
60|server worker is handling. You can treat ``request`` just like an actual
61|``Request`` object.
62|
63|``bool(proxy)`` will always return ``False`` if the var is not set. If
64|you need access to the object directly instead of the proxy, you can get
65|it with the :meth:`~LocalProxy._get_current_object` method.
66|
67|.. autoclass:: LocalProxy
68|    :members: _get_current_object
69|
70|
71|Stacks and Namespaces
72|=====================
73|
74|:class:`~contextvars.ContextVar` stores one value at a time. You may
75|find that you need to store a stack of items, or a namespace with
76|multiple attributes. A list or dict can be used for these, but using
77|them as context var values requires some extra care. Werkzeug provides
78|:class:`LocalStack` which wraps a list, and :class:`Local` which wraps a
79|dict.
80|
81|There is some amount of performance penalty associated with these
82|objects. Because lists and dicts are mutable, :class:`LocalStack` and
83|:class:`Local` need to do extra work to ensure data isn't shared between
84|nested contexts. If possible, design your application to use
85|:class:`LocalProxy` around a context var directly.
86|
87|.. autoclass:: LocalStack
88|    :members: push, pop, top, __call__
89|
90|.. autoclass:: Local
91|    :members: __call__
92|
93|
94|Releasing Data
95|==============
96|
97|A previous implementation of ``Local`` used internal data structures
98|which could not be cleaned up automatically when each context ended.
99|Instead, the following utilities could be used to release the data.
100|
101|.. warning::
102|
103|    This should not be needed with the modern implementation, as the
104|    data in context vars is automatically managed by Python. It is kept
105|    for compatibility for now, but may be removed in the future.
106|
107|.. autoclass:: LocalManager
108|   :members: cleanup, make_middleware, middleware
109|
110|.. autofunction:: release_local

3|HTTP Exceptions
4|===============
5|
6|These exceptions represent HTTP 4XX and 5XX error status codes. They can be
7|converted to an HTML response describing the error, and called as a WSGI
8|application to return that response.
9|
10|When using the :meth:`.Request.application` decorator to write an
11|application, it automatically catches all ``HTTPException`` errors and
12|returns their response. Other frameworks built on Werkzeug do this as well.
13|
14|.. code-block:: python
15|
16|    from werkzeug import Request, Response
17|    from werkzeug.exceptions import NotFound
18|
19|    @Request.application
20|    def app(request: Request) -> Response:
21|        if request.path != "/":
22|            raise NotFound()
23|
24|        return Response("Hello, World!")

115|Simple Aborting
116|---------------
117|
118|The ``abort`` function can be used to raise an exception by status code,
119|rather than importing the specific exception.
120|
121|.. autofunction:: abort
122|
123|If you want to use this with custom exceptions, create an instance of the
124|``Aborter`` class.

127|    :members: __call__

129|
130|Other Status Codes
131|------------------
132|
133|Werkzeug defines exceptions for many 4XX and 5XX error codes defined in modern
134|HTTP specs. If you need another error status as an exception, you can define
135|your own subclass.
136|
137|Status codes that do not represent errors are not defined as exceptions. 2XX
138|responses can be created directly with the :class:`.Response` class. Use
139|:func:`.redirect` to create 3XX redirect responses.
140|
141|To define a custom error, subclass :exc:`.HTTPException` and define the ``code``
142|class attribute. If Python's :class:`.HTTPStatus` defines that code, this is all
143|you need, it will pull the ``name`` and ``description`` from the enum.
144|Otherwise, define the ``name`` and ``description`` class attributes as well.
145|
146|    from werkzeug.exceptions import HTTPException
147|
148|    class PaymentRequired(HTTPException):
149|        code = 402
150|
151|If you want to add custom behavior, such as a required header, you can override
152|``__init__`` to take arguments, and :meth:`.HTTPException.get_response` to
153|customize the response.

8|functionality from this module is available on the high-level
9|:doc:`/wrappers`.
10|
11|

33|

46|-------------------

51|
52|
53|Bytes, Strings, and Encodings
54|-----------------------------
55|
56|The values in HTTP requests come in as bytes representing (or encoded
57|to) ASCII. The WSGI specification (:pep:`3333`) decided to always use
58|the ``str`` type to represent values. To accomplish this, the raw bytes
59|are decoded using the ISO-8859-1 charset to produce a string.
60|
61|Strings in the WSGI environment are restricted to ISO-8859-1 code
62|points. If a string read from the environment might contain characters
63|outside that charset, it must first be decoded to bytes as ISO-8859-1,
64|then encoded to a string using the proper charset (typically UTF-8). The
65|reverse is done when writing to the environ. This is known as the "WSGI
66|encoding dance".
67|
68|Werkzeug provides functions to deal with this automatically so that you
69|don't need to be aware of the inner workings. Use the functions on this
70|page as well as :func:`~werkzeug.datastructures.EnvironHeaders` to read
71|data out of the WSGI environment.
72|
73|Applications should avoid manually creating or modifying a WSGI
74|environment unless they take care of the proper encoding or decoding
75|step. All high level interfaces in Werkzeug will apply the encoding and
76|decoding as necessary.
77|
78|
79|Raw Request URI and Path Encoding
80|---------------------------------
81|
82|The ``PATH_INFO`` in the environ is the path value after
83|percent-decoding. For example, the raw path ``/hello%2fworld`` would
84|show up from the WSGI server to Werkzeug as ``/hello/world``. This loses
85|the information that the slash was a raw character as opposed to a path
86|separator.
87|
88|The WSGI specification (:pep:`3333`) does not provide a way to get the
89|original value, so it is impossible to route some types of data in the
90|path. The most compatible way to work around this is to send problematic
91|data in the query string instead of the path.
92|
93|However, many WSGI servers add a non-standard environ key with the raw
94|path. To match this behavior, Werkzeug's test client and development
95|server will add the raw value to both the ``REQUEST_URI`` and
96|``RAW_URI`` keys. If you want to route based on this value, you can use
97|middleware to replace ``PATH_INFO`` in the environ before it reaches the
98|application. However, keep in mind that these keys are non-standard and
99|not guaranteed to be present.
--- END FILE: docs/wsgi.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/test.rst ---
1|.. module:: werkzeug.test
2|
3|Testing WSGI Applications
4|=========================
5|
6|
7|Test Client
8|-----------
9|
10|Werkzeug provides a :class:`Client` to simulate requests to a WSGI
11|application without starting a server. The client has methods for making
12|different types of requests, as well as managing cookies across
13|requests.
14|
15|.. code-block:: python
16|
17|    from werkzeug import Request, Response, Client
18|
19|    @Request.application
20|    def app(request: Request) -> Response:
21|        return Response("Hello, World!")
22|
23|    c = Client(app)
24|    r = c.get("/")
25|    assert r.status_code == 200
26|    assert r.headers["Content-Type"] == "text/plain"
27|    assert r.text == "Hello, World!"
28|
29|The client's request methods return instances of :class:`TestResponse`.
30|This provides extra attributes and methods on top of
31|:class:`~werkzeug.wrappers.Response` that are useful for testing.
32|
33|
34|Request Body
35|------------
36|
37|By passing a dict to ``data``, the client will construct a request body
38|with file and form data. It will set the content type to
39|``application/x-www-form-urlencoded`` if there are no files, or
40|``multipart/form-data`` there are.
41|
42|.. code-block:: python
43|
44|    import io
45|
46|    response = client.post(data={
47|        "name": "test",
48|        "file": (BytesIO("file contents".encode("utf8")), "test.txt")
49|    })
50|
51|Pass a string, bytes, or file-like object to ``data`` to use that as the
52|raw request body. In that case, you should set the content type
53|appropriately. For example, to post YAML:
54|
55|.. code-block:: python
56|
57|    response = client.post(
58|        data="a: value\nb: 1\n", content_type="application/yaml"
59|    )
60|
61|A shortcut when testing JSON APIs is to pass a dict to ``json`` instead
62|of using ``data``. This will automatically call ``json.dumps()`` and
63|set the content type to ``application/json``. Additionally, if the
64|app returns JSON, ``response.json`` will automatically call
65|``json.loads()``.
66|
67|.. code-block:: python
68|
69|    response = client.post("/api", json={"a": "value", "b": 1})
70|    obj = response.json()
71|
72|
73|Environment Builder
74|-------------------
75|
76|:class:`EnvironBuilder` is used to construct a WSGI environ dict. The
77|test client uses this internally to prepare its requests. The arguments
78|passed to the client request methods are the same as the builder.
79|
80|Sometimes, it can be useful to construct a WSGI environment manually.
81|An environ builder or dict can be passed to the test client request
82|methods in place of other arguments to use a custom environ.
83|
84|.. code-block:: Python
85|
86|    from werkzeug.test import EnvironBuilder
87|    builder = EnvironBuilder(...)
88|    # build an environ dict
89|    environ = builder.get_environ()
90|    # build an environ dict wrapped in a request
91|    request = builder.get_request()
92|
93|The test client responses make this available through
94|:attr:`TestResponse.request` and ``response.request.environ``.
95|

1|Apache httpd
2|============
3|
4|`Apache httpd`_ is a fast, production level HTTP server. When serving
5|your application with one of the WSGI servers listed in :doc:`index`, it
6|is often good or necessary to put a dedicated HTTP server in front of
7|it. This "reverse proxy" can handle incoming requests, TLS, and other
8|security and performance concerns better than the WSGI server.
9|
10|httpd can be installed using your system package manager, or a pre-built
11|executable for Windows. Installing and running httpd itself is outside
12|the scope of this doc. This page outlines the basics of configuring
13|httpd to proxy your application. Be sure to read its documentation to
14|understand what features are available.
15|
16|.. _Apache httpd: https://httpd.apache.org/
17|
18|
19|Domain Name
20|-----------
21|
22|Acquiring and configuring a domain name is outside the scope of this
23|doc. In general, you will buy a domain name from a registrar, pay for
24|server space with a hosting provider, and then point your registrar
25|at the hosting provider's name servers.
26|
27|To simulate this, you can also edit your ``hosts`` file, located at
28|``/etc/hosts`` on Linux. Add a line that associates a name with the
29|local IP.
30|
31|Modern Linux systems may be configured to treat any domain name that
32|ends with ``.localhost`` like this without adding it to the ``hosts``
33|file.
34|
35|.. code-block:: python
36|    :caption: ``/etc/hosts``
37|
38|    127.0.0.1 hello.localhost
39|
40|
41|Configuration
42|-------------
43|
44|The httpd configuration is located at ``/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf`` on
45|Linux. It may be different depending on your operating system. Check the
46|docs and look for ``httpd.conf``.
47|
48|Remove or comment out any existing ``DocumentRoot`` directive. Add the
49|config lines below. We'll assume the WSGI server is listening locally at
50|``http://127.0.0.1:8000``.
51|
52|.. code-block:: apache
53|    :caption: ``/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf``
54|
55|    LoadModule proxy_module modules/mod_proxy.so
56|    LoadModule proxy_http_module modules/mod_proxy_http.so
57|    ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:8000/
58|    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto http
59|    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Prefix /
60|
61|The ``LoadModule`` lines might already exist. If so, make sure they are
62|uncommented instead of adding them manually.
63|
64|Then :doc:`proxy_fix` so that your application uses the ``X-Forwarded``
65|headers. ``X-Forwarded-For`` and ``X-Forwarded-Host`` are automatically
66|set by ``ProxyPass``.
67|
68|
69|Static Files
70|------------
71|
72|If your application has static files such as JavaScript, CSS, and
73|images, it will be more efficient to let Nginx serve them directly
74|rather than going through the Python application.
75|
76|Assuming the static files are expected to be available under the
77|``/static/`` URL, and are stored at ``/home/project/static/``, add the
78|following to the config above.
79|
80|.. code-block:: apache
81|
82|    Alias /static/ /home/project/static/
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/apache-httpd.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/deployment/mod_wsgi.rst ---
1|mod_wsgi
2|========
3|
4|`mod_wsgi`_ is a WSGI server integrated with the `Apache httpd`_ server.
5|The modern `mod_wsgi-express`_ command makes it easy to configure and
6|start the server without needing to write Apache httpd configuration.
7|
8|*   Tightly integrated with Apache httpd.
9|*   Supports Windows directly.
10|*   Requires a compiler and the Apache development headers to install.
11|*   Does not require a reverse proxy setup.
12|
13|This page outlines the basics of running mod_wsgi-express, not the more
14|complex installation and configuration with httpd. Be sure to read the
15|`mod_wsgi-express`_, `mod_wsgi`_, and `Apache httpd`_ documentation to
16|understand what features are available.
17|
18|.. _mod_wsgi-express: https://pypi.org/project/mod-wsgi/
19|.. _mod_wsgi: https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/
20|.. _Apache httpd: https://httpd.apache.org/
21|
22|
23|Installing
24|----------
25|
26|Installing mod_wsgi requires a compiler and the Apache server and
27|development headers installed. You will get an error if they are not.
28|How to install them depends on the OS and package manager that you use.
29|
30|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install
31|``mod_wsgi``.
32|
33|.. code-block:: text
34|
35|    $ cd hello-app
36|    $ python -m venv venv
37|    $ . venv/bin/activate
38|    $ pip install .  # install your application
39|    $ pip install mod_wsgi
40|
41|
42|Running
43|-------
44|
45|The only argument to ``mod_wsgi-express`` specifies a script containing
46|your application, which must be called ``application``. You can
47|write a small script to import your app with this name, or to create it
48|if using the app factory pattern.
49|
50|.. code-block:: python
51|    :caption: ``wsgi.py``
52|
53|    from hello import app
54|
55|    application = app
56|
57|.. code-block:: python
58|    :caption: ``wsgi.py``
59|
60|    from hello import create_app
61|
62|    application = create_app()
63|
64|Now run the ``mod_wsgi-express start-server`` command.
65|
66|.. code-block:: text
67|
68|    $ mod_wsgi-express start-server wsgi.py --processes 4
69|
70|The ``--processes`` option specifies the number of worker processes to
71|run; a starting value could be ``CPU * 2``.
72|
73|Logs for each request aren't show in the terminal. If an error occurs,
74|its information is written to the error log file shown when starting the
75|server.
76|
77|
78|Binding Externally
79|------------------
80|
81|Unlike the other WSGI servers in these docs, mod_wsgi can be run as
82|root to bind to privileged ports like 80 and 443. However, it must be
83|configured to drop permissions to a different user and group for the
84|worker processes.
85|
86|For example, if you created a ``hello`` user and group, you should
87|install your virtualenv and application as that user, then tell
88|mod_wsgi to drop to that user after starting.
89|
90|.. code-block:: text
91|
92|    $ sudo /home/hello/venv/bin/mod_wsgi-express start-server \
93|        /home/hello/wsgi.py \
94|        --user hello --group hello --port 80 --processes 4
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/mod_wsgi.rst ---

1|nginx
2|=====
3|
4|`nginx`_ is a fast, production level HTTP server. When serving your
5|application with one of the WSGI servers listed in :doc:`index`, it is
6|often good or necessary to put a dedicated HTTP server in front of it.
7|This "reverse proxy" can handle incoming requests, TLS, and other
8|security and performance concerns better than the WSGI server.
9|
10|Nginx can be installed using your system package manager, or a pre-built
11|executable for Windows. Installing and running Nginx itself is outside
12|the scope of this doc. This page outlines the basics of configuring
13|Nginx to proxy your application. Be sure to read its documentation to
14|understand what features are available.
15|
16|.. _nginx: https://nginx.org/
17|
18|
19|Domain Name
20|-----------
21|
22|Acquiring and configuring a domain name is outside the scope of this
23|doc. In general, you will buy a domain name from a registrar, pay for
24|server space with a hosting provider, and then point your registrar
25|at the hosting provider's name servers.
26|
27|To simulate this, you can also edit your ``hosts`` file, located at
28|``/etc/hosts`` on Linux. Add a line that associates a name with the
29|local IP.
30|
31|Modern Linux systems may be configured to treat any domain name that
32|ends with ``.localhost`` like this without adding it to the ``hosts``
33|file.
34|
35|.. code-block:: python
36|    :caption: ``/etc/hosts``
37|
38|    127.0.0.1 hello.localhost
39|
40|
41|Configuration
42|-------------
43|
44|The nginx configuration is located at ``/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`` on
45|Linux. It may be different depending on your operating system. Check the
46|docs and look for ``nginx.conf``.
47|
48|Remove or comment out any existing ``server`` section. Add a ``server``
49|section and use the ``proxy_pass`` directive to point to the address the
50|WSGI server is listening on. We'll assume the WSGI server is listening
51|locally at ``http://127.0.0.1:8000``.
52|
53|.. code-block:: nginx
54|    :caption: ``/etc/nginx.conf``
55|
56|    server {
57|        listen 80;
58|        server_name _;
59|
60|        location / {
61|            proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000/;
62|            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
63|            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
64|            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;
65|            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Prefix /;
66|        }
67|    }
68|
69|Then :doc:`proxy_fix` so that your application uses these headers.
70|
71|
72|Static Files
73|------------
74|
75|If your application has static files such as JavaScript, CSS, and
76|images, it will be more efficient to let Nginx serve them directly
77|rather than going through the Python application.
78|
79|Assuming the static files are expected to be available under the
80|``/static/`` URL, and are stored at ``/home/project/static/``, add the
81|following to the ``server`` block above.
82|
83|.. code-block:: nginx
84|
85|    location /static {
86|        alias /home/project/static;
87|    }
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/nginx.rst ---
--- FILE: README.md ---
1|<div align="center"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pallets/werkzeug/refs/heads/stable/docs/_static/werkzeug-name.svg" alt="" height="150"></div>
2|
3|# Werkzeug
4|
5|*werkzeug* German noun: "tool". Etymology: *werk* ("work"), *zeug* ("stuff")
6|
7|Werkzeug is a comprehensive [WSGI][] web application library. It began as
8|a simple collection of various utilities for WSGI applications and has
9|become one of the most advanced WSGI utility libraries.
10|
11|It includes:
12|
13|-   An interactive debugger that allows inspecting stack traces and
14|    source code in the browser with an interactive interpreter for any
15|    frame in the stack.
16|-   A full-featured request object with objects to interact with
17|    headers, query args, form data, files, and cookies.
18|-   A response object that can wrap other WSGI applications and handle
19|    streaming data.
20|-   A routing system for matching URLs to endpoints and generating URLs
21|    for endpoints, with an extensible system for capturing variables
22|    from URLs.
23|-   HTTP utilities to handle entity tags, cache control, dates, user
24|    agents, cookies, files, and more.
25|-   A threaded WSGI server for use while developing applications
26|    locally.
27|-   A test client for simulating HTTP requests during testing without
28|    requiring running a server.
29|
30|Werkzeug doesn't enforce any dependencies. It is up to the developer to
31|choose a template engine, database adapter, and even how to handle
32|requests. It can be used to build all sorts of end user applications
33|such as blogs, wikis, or bulletin boards.
34|
35|[Flask][] wraps Werkzeug, using it to handle the details of WSGI while
36|providing more structure and patterns for defining powerful
37|applications.
38|
39|[WSGI]: https://wsgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
40|[Flask]: https://www.palletsprojects.com/p/flask/
41|
42|
43|## A Simple Example
44|
45|```python
46|# save this as app.py
47|from werkzeug.wrappers import Request, Response
48|
49|
50|@Request.application
51|def application(request: Request) -> Response:
52|    return Response("Hello, World!")
53|
54|
55|if __name__ == "__main__":
56|    from werkzeug.serving import run_simple
57|
58|    run_simple("127.0.0.1", 5000, application)
59|```
60|
61|```
62|$ python -m app
63|  * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ (Press CTRL+C to quit)
64|```
65|
66|

--- FILE: docs/deployment/index.rst ---
1|Deploying to Production
2|=======================
3|
4|After developing your application, you'll want to make it available
5|publicly to other users. When you're developing locally, you're probably
6|using the built-in development server, debugger, and reloader. These
7|should not be used in production. Instead, you should use a dedicated
8|WSGI server or hosting platform, some of which will be described here.
9|
10|"Production" means "not development", which applies whether you're
11|serving your application publicly to millions of users or privately /
12|locally to a single user. **Do not use the development server when
13|deploying to production. It is intended for use only during local
14|development. It is not designed to be particularly secure, stable, or
15|efficient.**
16|
17|Self-Hosted Options
18|-------------------
19|
20|Werkzeug is a WSGI *application*. A WSGI *server* is used to run the
21|application, converting incoming HTTP requests to the standard WSGI
22|environ, and converting outgoing WSGI responses to HTTP responses.
23|
24|The primary goal of these docs is to familiarize you with the concepts
25|involved in running a WSGI application using a production WSGI server
26|and HTTP server. There are many WSGI servers and HTTP servers, with many
27|configuration possibilities. The pages below discuss the most common
28|servers, and show the basics of running each one. The next section
29|discusses platforms that can manage this for you.
30|
31|.. toctree::
32|    :maxdepth: 1
33|
34|    gunicorn
35|    waitress
36|    mod_wsgi
37|    uwsgi
38|    gevent
39|    eventlet
40|
41|WSGI servers have HTTP servers built-in. However, a dedicated HTTP
42|server may be safer, more efficient, or more capable. Putting an HTTP
43|server in front of the WSGI server is called a "reverse proxy."
44|
45|.. toctree::
46|    :maxdepth: 1
47|
48|    proxy_fix
49|    nginx
50|    apache-httpd
51|
52|This list is not exhaustive, and you should evaluate these and other
53|servers based on your application's needs. Different servers will have
54|different capabilities, configuration, and support.
55|
56|
57|Hosting Platforms
58|-----------------
59|
60|There are many services available for hosting web applications without
61|needing to maintain your own server, networking, domain, etc. Some
62|services may have a free tier up to a certain time or bandwidth. Many of
63|these services use one of the WSGI servers described above, or a similar
64|interface.
65|
66|You should evaluate services based on your application's needs.
67|Different services will have different capabilities, configuration,
68|pricing, and support.
69|
70|You'll probably need to :doc:`proxy_fix` when using most hosting
71|platforms.
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/index.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/deployment/gevent.rst ---
1|gevent
2|======
3|
4|Prefer using :doc:`gunicorn` or :doc:`uwsgi` with gevent workers rather
5|than using `gevent`_ directly. Gunicorn and uWSGI provide much more
6|configurable and production-tested servers.
7|
8|`gevent`_ allows writing asynchronous, coroutine-based code that looks
9|like standard synchronous Python. It uses `greenlet`_ to enable task
10|switching without writing ``async/await`` or using ``asyncio``.
11|
12|:doc:`eventlet` is another library that does the same thing. Certain
13|dependencies you have, or other considerations, may affect which of the
14|two you choose to use.
15|
16|gevent provides a WSGI server that can handle many connections at once
17|instead of one per worker process. You must actually use gevent in your
18|own code to see any benefit to using the server.
19|
20|.. _gevent: https://www.gevent.org/
21|.. _greenlet: https://greenlet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
22|
23|
24|Installing
25|----------
26|
27|When using gevent, greenlet>=1.0 is required, otherwise context locals
28|such as ``request`` will not work as expected. When using PyPy,
29|PyPy>=7.3.7 is required.
30|
31|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install ``gevent``.
32|
33|.. code-block:: text
34|
35|    $ cd hello-app
36|    $ python -m venv venv
37|    $ . venv/bin/activate
38|    $ pip install .  # install your application
39|    $ pip install gevent
40|
41|
42|Running
43|-------
44|
45|To use gevent to serve your application, write a script that imports its
46|``WSGIServer``, as well as your app or app factory.
47|
48|.. code-block:: python
49|    :caption: ``wsgi.py``
50|
51|    from gevent.pywsgi import WSGIServer
52|    from hello import create_app
53|
54|    app = create_app()
55|    http_server = WSGIServer(("127.0.0.1", 8000), app)
56|    http_server.serve_forever()
57|
58|.. code-block:: text
59|
60|    $ python wsgi.py
61|
62|No output is shown when the server starts.
63|
64|
65|Binding Externally
66|------------------
67|
68|gevent should not be run as root because it would cause your
69|application code to run as root, which is not secure. However, this
70|means it will not be possible to bind to port 80 or 443. Instead, a
71|reverse proxy such as :doc:`nginx` or :doc:`apache-httpd` should be used
72|in front of gevent.
73|
74|You can bind to all external IPs on a non-privileged port by using
75|``0.0.0.0`` in the server arguments shown in the previous section. Don't
76|do this when using a reverse proxy setup, otherwise it will be possible
77|to bypass the proxy.
78|
79|``0.0.0.0`` is not a valid address to navigate to, you'd use a specific
80|IP address in your browser.
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/gevent.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/deployment/eventlet.rst ---
1|eventlet
2|========
3|
4|Prefer using :doc:`gunicorn` with eventlet workers rather than using
5|`eventlet`_ directly. Gunicorn provides a much more configurable and
6|production-tested server.
7|
8|`eventlet`_ allows writing asynchronous, coroutine-based code that looks
9|like standard synchronous Python. It uses `greenlet`_ to enable task
10|switching without writing ``async/await`` or using ``asyncio``.
11|
12|:doc:`gevent` is another library that does the same thing. Certain
13|dependencies you have, or other considerations, may affect which of the
14|two you choose to use.
15|
16|eventlet provides a WSGI server that can handle many connections at once
17|instead of one per worker process. You must actually use eventlet in
18|your own code to see any benefit to using the server.
19|
20|.. _eventlet: https://eventlet.net/
21|.. _greenlet: https://greenlet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
22|
23|
24|Installing
25|----------
26|
27|When using eventlet, greenlet>=1.0 is required, otherwise context locals
28|such as ``request`` will not work as expected. When using PyPy,
29|PyPy>=7.3.7 is required.
30|
31|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install
32|``eventlet``.
33|
34|.. code-block:: text
35|
36|    $ cd hello-app
37|    $ python -m venv venv
38|    $ . venv/bin/activate
39|    $ pip install .  # install your application
40|    $ pip install eventlet
41|
42|
43|Running
44|-------
45|
46|To use eventlet to serve your application, write a script that imports
47|its ``wsgi.server``, as well as your app or app factory.
48|
49|.. code-block:: python
50|    :caption: ``wsgi.py``
51|
52|    import eventlet
53|    from eventlet import wsgi
54|    from hello import create_app
55|
56|    app = create_app()
57|    wsgi.server(eventlet.listen(("127.0.0.1", 8000), app)
58|
59|.. code-block:: text
60|
61|    $ python wsgi.py
62|    (x) wsgi starting up on http://127.0.0.1:8000
63|
64|
65|Binding Externally
66|------------------
67|
68|eventlet should not be run as root because it would cause your
69|application code to run as root, which is not secure. However, this
70|means it will not be possible to bind to port 80 or 443. Instead, a
71|reverse proxy such as :doc:`nginx` or :doc:`apache-httpd` should be used
72|in front of eventlet.
73|
74|You can bind to all external IPs on a non-privileged port by using
75|``0.0.0.0`` in the server arguments shown in the previous section.
76|Don't do this when using a reverse proxy setup, otherwise it will be
77|possible to bypass the proxy.
78|
79|``0.0.0.0`` is not a valid address to navigate to, you'd use a specific
80|IP address in your browser.
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/eventlet.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/deployment/waitress.rst ---
1|Waitress
2|========
3|
4|`Waitress`_ is a pure Python WSGI server.
5|
6|*   It is easy to configure.
7|*   It supports Windows directly.
8|*   It is easy to install as it does not require additional dependencies
9|    or compilation.
10|*   It does not support streaming requests, full request data is always
11|    buffered.
12|*   It uses a single process with multiple thread workers.
13|
14|This page outlines the basics of running Waitress. Be sure to read its
15|documentation and ``waitress-serve --help`` to understand what features
16|are available.
17|
18|.. _Waitress: https://docs.pylonsproject.org/projects/waitress/
19|
20|
21|Installing
22|----------
23|
24|Create a virtualenv, install your application, then install
25|``waitress``.
26|
27|.. code-block:: text
28|
29|    $ cd hello-app
30|    $ python -m venv venv
31|    $ . venv/bin/activate
32|    $ pip install .  # install your application
33|    $ pip install waitress
34|
35|
36|Running
37|-------
38|
39|The only required argument to ``waitress-serve`` tells it how to load
40|your application. The syntax is ``{module}:{app}``. ``module`` is
41|the dotted import name to the module with your application. ``app`` is
42|the variable with the application. If you're using the app factory
43|pattern, use ``--call {module}:{factory}`` instead.
44|
45|.. code-block:: text
46|
47|    # equivalent to 'from hello import app'
48|    $ waitress-serve hello:app --host 127.0.0.1
49|
50|    # equivalent to 'from hello import create_app; create_app()'
51|    $ waitress-serve --call hello:create_app --host 127.0.0.1
52|
53|    Serving on http://127.0.0.1:8080
54|
55|The ``--host`` option binds the server to local ``127.0.0.1`` only.
56|
57|Logs for each request aren't shown, only errors are shown. Logging can
58|be configured through the Python interface instead of the command line.
59|
60|
61|Binding Externally
62|------------------
63|
64|Waitress should not be run as root because it would cause your
65|application code to run as root, which is not secure. However, this
66|means it will not be possible to bind to port 80 or 443. Instead, a
67|reverse proxy such as :doc:`nginx` or :doc:`apache-httpd` should be used
68|in front of Waitress.
69|
70|You can bind to all external IPs on a non-privileged port by not
71|specifying the ``--host`` option. Don't do this when using a revers
72|proxy setup, otherwise it will be possible to bypass the proxy.
73|
74|``0.0.0.0`` is not a valid address to navigate to, you'd use a specific
75|IP address in your browser.
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/waitress.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/installation.rst ---
1|Installation
2|============
3|
4|
5|Python Version
6|--------------
7|
8|We recommend using the latest version of Python. Werkzeug supports
9|Python 3.11 and newer.
10|
11|
12|Optional dependencies
13|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
14|
15|These distributions will not be installed automatically. Werkzeug will
16|detect and use them if you install them.
17|
18|* `Watchdog`_ provides a faster, more efficient reloader for the
19|  development server.
20|
21|.. _Watchdog: https://pypi.org/project/watchdog/
22|
23|
24|greenlet
25|~~~~~~~~
26|
27|You may choose to use gevent or eventlet with your application. In this
28|case, greenlet>=1.0 is required. When using PyPy, PyPy>=7.3.7 is
29|required.
30|
31|These are not minimum supported versions, they only indicate the first
32|versions that added necessary features. You should use the latest
33|versions of each.
34|
35|
36|Virtual environments
37|--------------------
38|
39|Use a virtual environment to manage the dependencies for your project,
40|both in development and in production.
41|
42|What problem does a virtual environment solve? The more Python
43|projects you have, the more likely it is that you need to work with
44|different versions of Python libraries, or even Python itself. Newer
45|versions of libraries for one project can break compatibility in
46|another project.
47|
48|Virtual environments are independent groups of Python libraries, one for
49|each project. Packages installed for one project will not affect other
50|projects or the operating system's packages.
51|
52|Python comes bundled with the :mod:`venv` module to create virtual
53|environments.
54|
55|
56|Create an environment
57|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
58|
59|Create a project folder and a :file:`venv` folder within:
60|
61|.. code-block:: sh
62|
63|    mkdir myproject
64|    cd myproject
65|    python3 -m venv venv
66|
67|On Windows:
68|
69|.. code-block:: bat
70|
71|    py -3 -m venv venv
72|
73|
74|Activate the environment
75|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
76|
77|Before you work on your project, activate the corresponding environment:
78|
79|.. code-block:: sh
80|
81|    . venv/bin/activate
82|
83|On Windows:
84|
85|.. code-block:: bat
86|
87|    venv\Scripts\activate
88|
89|Your shell prompt will change to show the name of the activated
90|environment.
91|
92|
93|Install Werkzeug
94|----------------
95|
96|Within the activated environment, use the following command to install
97|Werkzeug:
98|
99|.. code-block:: sh
100|
101|    pip install Werkzeug

--- FILE: docs/terms.rst ---
1|===============
2|Important Terms
3|===============
4|
5|.. currentmodule:: werkzeug
6|
7|This page covers important terms used in the documentation and Werkzeug
8|itself.
9|
10|
11|WSGI
12|----
13|
14|WSGI a specification for Python web applications Werkzeug follows.  It was
15|specified in the :pep:`3333` and is widely supported.  Unlike previous solutions
16|it guarantees that web applications, servers and utilities can work together.
17|
18|Response Object
19|---------------
20|
21|For Werkzeug, a response object is an object that works like a WSGI
22|application but does not do any request processing.  Usually you have a view
23|function or controller method that processes the request and assembles a
24|response object.
25|
26|A response object is *not* necessarily the :class:`Response` class or a
27|subclass thereof.
28|
29|For example Pylons/webob provide a very similar response class that can
30|be used as well (:class:`webob.Response`).
31|
32|View Function
33|-------------
34|
35|Often people speak of MVC (Model, View, Controller) when developing web
36|applications.  However, the Django framework coined MTV (Model, Template,
37|View) which basically means the same but reduces the concept to the data
38|model, a function that processes data from the request and the database and
39|renders a template.
40|
41|Werkzeug itself does not tell you how you should develop applications, but the
42|documentation often speaks of view functions that work roughly the same.  The
43|idea of a view function is that it's called with a request object (and
44|optionally some parameters from an URL rule) and returns a response object.
--- END FILE: docs/terms.rst ---

--- FILE: docs/deployment/proxy_fix.rst ---
1|Tell Werkzeug it is Behind a Proxy
2|==================================
3|
4|When using a reverse proxy, or many Python hosting platforms, the proxy
5|will intercept and forward all external requests to the local WSGI
6|server.
7|
8|From the WSGI server and application's perspectives, requests are now
9|coming from the HTTP server to the local address, rather than from
10|the remote address to the external server address.
11|
12|HTTP servers should set ``X-Forwarded-`` headers to pass on the real
13|values to the application. The application can then be told to trust and
14|use those values by wrapping it with the
15|:doc:`../middleware/proxy_fix` middleware provided by Werkzeug.
16|
17|This middleware should only be used if the application is actually
18|behind a proxy, and should be configured with the number of proxies that
19|are chained in front of it. Not all proxies set all the headers. Since
20|incoming headers can be faked, you must set how many proxies are setting
21|each header so the middleware knows what to trust.
22|
23|.. code-block:: python
24|
25|    from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix import ProxyFix
26|
27|    app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(
28|        app.wsgi_app, x_for=1, x_proto=1, x_host=1, x_prefix=1
29|    )
30|
31|Remember, only apply this middleware if you are behind a proxy, and set
32|the correct number of proxies that set each header. It can be a security
33|issue if you get this configuration wrong.
--- END FILE: docs/deployment/proxy_fix.rst ---

88|            int, bits[4:8]

34|    function in web.py
35|    """

37|    def __init__(self, urls, views):
38|        self.urls = [
39|            (re.compile(f"^{urls[i]}$"), urls[i + 1]) for i in range(0, len(urls), 2)
40|        ]
41|        self.views = views

50|                    if req.method not in ("GET", "HEAD", "POST", "DELETE", "PUT"):
51|                        raise NotImplemented()  # noqa: F901

1|"""A simple object database. As long as the server is not running in
2|multiprocess mode that's good enough.
3|"""
4|import dbm
5|from pickle import dumps
6|from pickle import loads
7|from threading import Lock
8|
9|
10|class Database:
11|    def __init__(self, filename):
12|        self.filename = filename
13|        self._fs = dbm.open(filename, "cf")
14|        self._local = {}
15|        self._lock = Lock()
16|
17|    def __getitem__(self, key):
18|        with self._lock:
19|            return self._load_key(key)
20|
21|    def _load_key(self, key):
22|        if key in self._local:
23|            return self._local[key]
24|        rv = loads(self._fs[key])
25|        self._local[key] = rv
26|        return rv
27|
28|    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
29|        self._local[key] = value
30|
31|    def __delitem__(self, key):
32|        with self._lock:
33|            self._local.pop(key, None)
34|            if key in self._fs:
35|                del self._fs[key]
36|
37|    def __del__(self):
38|        self.close()
39|
40|    def __contains__(self, key):
41|        with self._lock:
42|            try:
43|                self._load_key(key)
44|            except KeyError:
45|                pass
46|            return key in self._local
47|
48|    def setdefault(self, key, factory):
49|        with self._lock:
50|            try:
51|                rv = self._load_key(key)
52|            except KeyError:
53|                self._local[key] = rv = factory()
54|            return rv
55|
56|    def sync(self):
57|        with self._lock:
58|            for key, value in self._local.items():
59|                self._fs[key] = dumps(value, 2)
60|            self._fs.sync()
61|
62|    def close(self):
63|        try:
64|            self.sync()
65|            self._fs.close()
66|        except Exception:
67|            pass

702|def make_call_asserter(func=None):
703|    """Utility to assert a certain number of function calls.
704|
705|    :param func: Additional callback for each function call.
706|
707|    .. code-block:: python
708|        assert_calls, func = make_call_asserter()
709|        with assert_calls(2):
710|            func()
711|            func()
712|    """
713|    calls = [0]
714|
715|    @contextmanager
716|    def asserter(count, msg=None):
717|        calls[0] = 0
718|        yield
719|        assert calls[0] == count
720|
721|    def wrapped(*args, **kwargs):
722|        calls[0] += 1
723|        if func is not None:
724|            return func(*args, **kwargs)
725|
726|    return asserter, wrapped
